“I was having a really difficult time passing classes and was really burned out,” said Castro-Chavez, 23, a communications studies major who hopes to become a public school teacher. “And I’ve lost four family members to Covid now. It hit me pretty hard.”

As that fall semester wrapped up, Castro-Chavez, who had recently tested positive for Covid herself after losing her aunt and cousins, told her adviser she wasn’t sure she’d be back. The adviser encouraged her to take a short break and then return to school slowly, maybe just taking a couple of classes to start.

The pep talk worked. Castro-Chavez took the spring semester off and focused on her trucking company job. But this past August she re-enrolled, first with a course load of two classes, and then, this semester, three.

It can be challenging getting any student back on track after time off. Just 2 percent of 2020 high school graduates who [did not immediately enroll in college](https://www.studentclearinghouse.org/blog/high-school-benchmarks-2021-report-features-gap-year-enrollment-analysis/) showed up in fall 2021, according to the National Student Clearinghouse Research Center. The center also found that 30,600 [fewer transfer students](https://nscresearchcenter.org/transfer-mobility-and-progress/) who took time off from college returned this past fall, a drop of 5.8 percent from the year before.

**Related:**[**‘It’s just too much’: Why students are abandoning community colleges in droves**](https://hechingerreport.org/its-just-too-much-why-students-are-abandoning-community-colleges-in-droves/)

Maggie Callow, 19, bucked those national trends but said it was tough to get into the college mindset after taking a pandemic-induced gap year last year. Having struggled with online classes her final two months of high school in 2020, she just couldn’t fathom spending her first year of college online. So she spent the year at home in Bozeman, Montana, working in a pizza shop, hiking and taking a French class at Montana State University.

Now halfway through her freshman year at Pomona College in Southern California, Callow was deeply disappointed when the college announced the first two weeks of the spring semester would be online. A lot of her classmates are having trouble, she said.

“I think a lot fewer people are going to graduate from college,” she said.

Izzy B., the 18-year-old from Colorado, said she wants to return to college eventually, to become a therapist. But for now, she’s working on her mental well-being.

“We just don’t take mental health seriously,” said Izzy. “It wasn’t until I was thinking, ‘Oh, I’m going to kill myself,’ ” she said, that she realized she needed to take action to care for herself. “That was a very concrete point.”

# How Charlie Kirk went from college dropout to Trump influencer

[Analysis](https://baptistnews.com/category/analysis/)[Mara Richards Bim](https://baptistnews.com/article/author/mrbim/)| April 15, 2025

![Image 4](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/AP24276792369838.jpg?resize=1200%2C500&ssl=1)

i

Donald Trump shakes hands with Turning Point CEO Charlie Kirk before speaking during the Turning Point USA Student Action Summit, Saturday, July 23, 2022, in Tampa, Fla. (AP Photo/Phelan M. Ebenhack)

_From BNG’s coverage earlier this year, first published April 15, 2025:_

**It seems Charlie Kirk — the Millennial founder** of the Christian nationalist powerhouse Turning Point USA — is everywhere these days.

He was part of a handful of Trump insiders tasked last fall with [administering](https://www.yahoo.com/news/charlie-kirk-conducting-loyalty-tests-184500064.html)[loyalty tests](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/12/07/us/politics/trump-administration-loyalty-test.html) to prospective hires for senior posts at the Pentagon and within the intelligence agencies.

More recently, Kirk, now 31, was one of a number of [loyalists](https://www.politico.com/news/2025/03/17/michael-flynn-charlie-kirk-trump-appointments-00234637) President Trump appointed to the boards of the military academies in the United States. Kirk was appointed to the Air Force Academy’s [Board of Visitors](https://www.usafa.edu/about/bov/) charged with inquiring into, among other things, the academy’s curriculum and instruction.

Kirk’s appointment is especially ironic. It was his [rejection](https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2022/10/20/charlie-kirks-republican-friends-00062305) from West Point Military Academy as a graduating senior in 2012 from Wheeling High School outside of Chicago that sent him on a downward spiral and into the arms of the burgeoning right-wing extremist movement which he now sits at the top of.

#### **The beginnings of Charlie Kirk**

In her book _Raising Them Right: The Untold Story of America’s Ultraconservative Youth Movement and its Plot for Power_, journalist Kyle Spencer sums up Kirk’s trajectory within the politics of resentment: “His metamorphosis can be seen as a case study of the power of grievance politics and a reminder that resentment is an energizing fuel most potent when delivered by leaders who have felt it deeply themselves.”

[![Image 5](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/i-went-to-high-school-with-charlie-kirk-v0-rclmfa50fhfc1.jpeg.jpg?resize=207%2C300&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/i-went-to-high-school-with-charlie-kirk-v0-rclmfa50fhfc1.jpeg.jpg?ssl=1)
Charlie Kirk as a high school senior

Kirk’s father was an architect with his own firm. He designed and built middle-class luxury estates while Kirk’s mother traded at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (she later went back to school to become a licensed therapist). Undoubtedly the 2008 housing crisis and the resulting bank bailouts impacted the Kirks’ businesses and was fodder for dinner table conversation in their five-bedroom mansion.

Kirk’s resentment was in full-bloom a few months later at the start of his freshman year under the new Obama presidency. Obama’s career began in the same Chicago suburb where Kirk attended high school. While the first African American president’s political win was celebrated by most in the rapidly diversifying suburb, it was not celebrated by Kirk.

Whether it was Obama’s continuance of George W. Bush’s bank bailouts or his skin color, Kirk was not a fan. In response, he began building a contrarian political persona around his freshman interpretation of Reagan economics, the work of the economist Milton Friedman and gun rights.

Kirk’s classmates described him as “rude,” “arrogant” and as someone with “a superiority complex.” He called teachers with whom he disagreed “neo-Marxists” and often was belligerent in class. On the topic of gun rights, Spencer [writes](https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2022/10/20/charlie-kirks-republican-friends-00062305) that Kirk “once asked a teacher if guns make people violent, ‘do forks make people fat?’”

By the time Kirk entered his senior year, the Tea Party was on the rise. Stanford sociologist Robb Willer conducted a [study](https://news.stanford.edu/stories/2016/05/perceived-threats-racial-status-drive-white-americans-support-tea-party-stanford-scholar-says) in 2016 that showed the rise of the Tea Party was directly linked to “the relative ‘racial standing’ of whites in the United States” with the election of Obama and the economic trends around 2008.

As a high school senior, Kirk began going to meetings and hanging out with right-wing political activists like 71-year old [Bill Montgomery](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/02/10/magazine/charlie-kirk-american-right.html) who, months later, would help Kirk co-found Turning Point USA. Also during his senior year, Kirk wrote an [opinion piece](https://dartreview.com/a-profile-of-charlie-kirk/) for the [controversial](https://bridge.georgetown.edu/research/factsheet-breitbart-news/)[misinformation](https://democracyforward.org/work/investigation-misinformation/) site Breitbart News, which landed him an interview on Fox News.

As he headed toward graduation, Kirk was denied entry into West Point — one of the most selective universities in America, with an [acceptance rate](https://www.prepscholar.com/sat/s/colleges/West-Point-admission-requirements#:~:text=The%20acceptance%20rate%20at%20West,and%20proving%20your%20academic%20preparation.) of 12%.

Kirk, however, [claimed](https://dartreview.com/a-profile-of-charlie-kirk/) his rejection was because he was passed over for “a far less-qualified candidate of a different gender and a different persuasion.”

[![Image 6](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/maxresdefault-43.jpg?resize=382%2C215&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/maxresdefault-43.jpg?ssl=1)
Social media post noting the death of Bill Montgomery.

Montgomery convinced him to take a gap year and work the political circuit. Using money he received for his high school graduation, Kirk launched TPUSA with Montgomery. He was 18 years old.

Kirk briefly attended[Harper College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harper_College), a community college near Chicago, but dropped out and never completed a degree.

#### **Politics of resentment**

In the fall of 2012 — just months after graduating high school — Kirk and TPUSA began by [sponsoring debates](https://www.newspapers.com/image/75778781) between Democratic and Republican students on a handful of college campuses in the Midwest. He also attended the Republican National Convention, where a chance meeting with multimillionaire investor Foster Freiss in a stairwell led to an infusion of cash into TPUSA.

After Obama won a second term in fall 2012, Kirk and TPUSA became integral to the infighting within the Republican Party. Kirk spent the next three years touring the country to speak at a variety of Republican — and primarily Tea Party — events. The Tea Party — having seen Republicans lose again in the 2012 presidential election — was livid and organizing. The target of their vitriol was the Affordable Care Act (which they dubbed “Obamacare”) and they were mobilizing to take over the Republican Party.

It was in these Tea Party meeting rooms that Kirk — a teenage, angry white male — learned to work a room and engage with political donors.

One such event was in June 2013 with then-Congressman Steve Daines (now senator), Montana’s then-Attorney General Tim Fox (who left office in [disgrace](https://flatheadbeacon.com/2020/12/23/what-an-embarrassment/) after signing onto a lawsuit challenging the 2020 election results) and former Montana Sen. Ryan Zinke (who later served as Trump’s first secretary of the interior and is now a representative for Montana).

[![Image 7](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/61369370.jpg?resize=245%2C375&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/61369370.jpg?ssl=1)Quoted afterward in _[The Montana Standard](https://www.newspapers.com/image/471013795),_ Kirk said he started TPUSA and was hanging out with right-wing Tea Party activists specifically because he was frustrated with the “too bureaucratic” Young Republicans who were unwilling to try new approaches to organizing.

By the time Donald J. Trump came onto the scene, Kirk had secured a spot within the remade Republican Party. More important, after marinating in resentment politics for several years, Kirk was a true believer.

Much has been written about Trump’s success at tapping into this grievance culture. Kirk, like many young white men who did not attend college, relished Trump’s offensive behavior and rhetoric. They felt “seen” again. And they began acting out and amplifying the behavior of their new leader.

#### **Charlie Kirk, Donald Trump and neo-Nazis**

On June 16, 2015, Trump made his [infamous descent](https://www.washingtonpost.com/video/politics/2015-trump-launches-presidential-campaign/2019/06/17/8e8d7747-e028-4f89-8e30-78d7311827e8_video.html) down the escalator at Trump Tower in New York City to officially launch his 2016 campaign. His inaugural speech was filled with the kind of [racist rhetoric](https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-election-trump/with-barbs-and-bluster-trump-barges-into-2016-white-house-race-idUSKBN0OW1ZU20150618/) he had become known for after five years of [falsely](https://www.wsj.com/articles/BL-WB-65498) saying Barack Obama was not born in America.

The next day, a 21-year old white supremacist neo-Nazi attended a Bible study at Mother Emanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church in Charleston, S.C. At the end of the study, he stood up and [opened fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charleston_church_shooting) on the 10 African American church members who had opened their community to him — killing nine of them, including the senior pastor, state senator Clementa C. Pinckney.

These events — Trump’s racist campaign, the mass shooting at a historic African American church and the platforming of a young, angry white Charlie Kirk — are in many ways the starting point for where we are in today’s political landscape filled with conspiracy theories and the rise of Christian nationalism.

Weeks after the Mother Emanuel shootings, Kirk joined the Trump campaign, where he became friends with the future president’s son, Donald Trump Jr. He also launched Turning Point Action Inc., a 501(c)(4) tied to his nonprofit TPUSA. The new nonprofit strategically placed him within the [web of dark money](https://baptistnews.com/article/want-to-know-whos-behind-project-2025-follow-the-money-through-the-swamp/) that [continues](https://baptistnews.com/article/following-leonard-leos-dark-money-in-pushing-america-to-the-far-right/) to this day.

[![Image 8](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/06/ezgif.com-gif-maker-70.jpg?resize=300%2C280&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/06/ezgif.com-gif-maker-70.jpg?ssl=1)
Charlie Kirk with Jerry Falwell Jr. in a publicity photo for the Falkirk Center at Liberty University. The name was a mash up for Falwell and Kirk.

After Trump’s surprise victory in 2016, Kirk and TPUSA upped the ante on their provocative antics by publishing a “[Professor Watchlist](https://www.newspapers.com/image/656391804/).” The list targeted college professors who [Kirk accused](https://www.newspapers.com/image/364943350/) (without evidence) of promoting undefined “leftist propaganda.”

Individuals from across the political spectrum decried the move and called it a “[witch hunt](https://www.newspapers.com/image/1077717863/)” and [reminiscent](https://www.newspapers.com/image/693557361/) of Sen. Joseph McCarthy’s [political persecution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCarthyism) of anyone he thought might be a communist.

This list was just TPUSA’s opening salvo in an escalating war on college campuses; but the war on college campuses wasn’t the only war raging in the early days of the Trump presidency. In the aftermath of the Mother Emanuel mass shooting and anti-Black hate crime, calls echoed across the South to once and for all [remove the monuments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Removal_of_Confederate_monuments_and_memorials) erected to memorialize the Confederacy from the Civil War.

These [monuments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederate_monuments_and_memorials) — raised up during and after the height of Jim Crow laws — continued to feed the [Lost Cause](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lost_Cause_of_the_Confederacy) narrative embraced by white supremacists. That [myth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lost_Cause_of_the_Confederacy) — that the heroic Confederacy rose up to justly fight the Civil War as an act of liberty rather than over slavery — has influenced every facet of life in the South since it was first deployed in 1866.

In the first year of Trump’s presidency, fueled in no small part by the president’s continued racist rhetoric, battles over Confederate monuments reached a fevered pitch.

On Aug. 11, 2017, after weeks of [publicizing](https://www.nytimes.com/2018/08/12/us/politics/charlottesville-va-protest-unite-the-right.html) it, white supremacist and neo-Nazi groups descended on the streets of [Charlottesville, Va.,](https://time.com/charlottesville-white-nationalist-rally-clashes/) under the [pretense](https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/archive/2017/08/nazis-racism-charlottesville/536928/) of protesting the removal of a statue of Robert E. Lee. Angry white men marched through the streets carrying tiki torches and shouting slogans like “Jews will not replace us.”

While young, angry white supremacist neo-Nazis were taking to the streets in cities like Charlottesville, they were beginning to take note of Kirk and TPUSA.

After releasing the “Professor Watchlist,” Kirk and TPUSA began [booking appearances](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2017/jan/28/milo-yiannopoulos-campus-speaking-tour-colorado) with alt-right neo-Nazis like Milo Yiannopoulos. These campus appearances led to massive (and [sometimes violent](https://www.cnn.com/2017/02/01/us/milo-yiannopoulos-berkeley/index.html)) protests on college campuses.

After Charlottesville, white supremacists and neo-Nazis flocked to TPUSA events on college campuses and elsewhere, looking to fight with counter protesters. Kirk did [nothing](https://truthout.org/articles/young-fascists-on-campus-turning-point-usa-and-its-far-right-connections/) to separate himself or TPUSA from them.

> “After Charlottesville, white supremacists and neo-Nazis flocked to TPUSA events on college campuses.”

In fact, many of TPUSA’s field organizers embraced the white supremacists in their midst. So much so that the media started taking note. Rather than distancing itself from racists and neo-Nazis, Kirk and TPUSA began offering “new and former staff with complimentary [social media background checks](https://www.huffpost.com/entry/turning-point-usa-racist-tweets_n_5ad65b06e4b029ebe01ed1ac)” to uncover past racist behavior “that could potentially damage your credibility or the credibility of the organization.”

TPUSA had become a powerhouse in national politics and Kirk didn’t want to see the organization brought down by inconvenient ties to racism.

For example, during the 2018 midterms, Turning Point Action Inc. and TPUSA both engaged the marketing firm Rally Forge to place ads from a fake liberal organization and to create a troll farm on Facebook to [promote Republican candidates](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2021/jun/11/facebook-ads-turning-point-usa-rally-forge). From July 2018 to June 2019, the two organizations paid Rally Forge nearly $1 million for the ads.

[![Image 9](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/52147677176_f76c3a7f46_o.jpg?resize=1700%2C1040&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/52147677176_f76c3a7f46_o.jpg?ssl=1)
Charlie Kirk speaks to a gathering sponsored by the Conservative Baptist Network during the SBC annual meeting.

#### **Kirk embraces Christian nationalism**

In the years between Trump’s 2020 election defeat and his 2024 campaign, Kirk found himself at odds with neo-Nazi groups. To their mind, TPUSA wasn’t [racist enough](https://www.dailydot.com/debug/charlie-kirk-white-nationalist-nick-fuentes-turning-point-usa/). That didn’t keep Kirk or TPUSA from [schmoozing with them](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/nazis-mingle-openly-cpac-spreading-antisemitic-conspiracy-theories-fin-rcna140335) at events like the Conservative Political Action Conference. Nevertheless, Kirk and TPUSA sought to distance themselves publicly from neo-Nazism. As they did, they moved toward a full-throated embrace of [Christian nationalism](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2024-election/charlie-kirk-turning-point-donald-trump-christian-nationalism-rcna156565).

Recently, there have been several [articles](https://www.rollingstone.com/politics/politics-features/charlie-kirk-turning-point-usa-pivots-to-christian-nationalism-1234740083/) noting the [evolution](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2024-election/charlie-kirk-turning-point-donald-trump-christian-nationalism-rcna156565) of Kirk and TPUSA from an organization devoted to promoting free market capitalism to one focused on promoting Christian nationalism.

In 2018, during an [interview](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FhCKfxy83BQ&t=166s) titled “Defending Christianity and Discussing Radical Islam,” Kirk told conservative commentator Dave Rubin Christians should respect the separation of church and state. But in 2022, Kirk — in his own podcast — [declared](https://www.mediamatters.org/charlie-kirk/charlie-kirk-there-no-separation-church-and-state): “There is no separation of church and state. It’s a fabrication. It’s a fiction. It’s not in the Constitution. It’s made up by secular humanists. It’s derived from a single letter that Thomas Jefferson wrote to the Danbury Baptist Convention.”

This assertion is a nearly word-for-word talking point from the controversial pseudo-historian [David Barton](https://www.texastribune.org/2022/07/29/texas-church-state-separation-opposition/).

[![Image 10](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/AP24167249757668.jpg?resize=300%2C200&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/AP24167249757668.jpg?ssl=1)
An attendee shows off his copy of Right Wing Revolution by Charlie Kirk at The People’s Convention hosted by Turning Point USA in Detroit on June 14, 2024. (Photo by Adam J. Dewey/NurPhoto via AP)

On TPUSA’s 2021 tax filing, TPUSA [redefined its mission](https://apps.irs.gov/pub/epostcard/cor/800835023_202206_990_2023060921420938.pdf) for the first time since its founding. Now, just months after the January 6 attempted insurrection, TPUSA was no longer focused on “fiscal responsibility, free markets and capitalism through non-partisan debate, dialogue and discussion.” Instead, TPUSA identified its mission as:

_To empower informed civic and cultural engagement grounded in American Exceptionalism and a positive spirit of action. Turning Point USA guides citizens through development of knowledge, skills, values and motivation, so they can meaningfully engage in their communities to restore traditional American values like patriotism, respect for life, liberty, family and fiscal responsibility._

The 2021 tax filing also is the first one in which TPUSA listed as one of its programs “TPUSA Faith.” TPUSA received a $50,000 gift in the early part of 2022 from [It Takes a Family Foundation](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/582276414) — a right-wing, NAR-supporting family foundation that also funds the extremist groups Family Research Council, Project Veritas, Judicial Watch, Sean Feucht’s Let Us Worship and Barton’s Wallbuilders, among others.

[![Image 11](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/CouragerTour.jpg?resize=2200%2C916&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/CouragerTour.jpg?ssl=1)
Screenshot from Courage Tour website

In fact, it seems the family members behind It Takes a Family Foundation are the connection between Kirk’s TPUSA, Sean Feucht’s ministry and NAR frontman Lance Wallnau. Together, these three men created “[The Courage Tour](https://www.rollingstone.com/politics/politics-features/christian-nationalists-churches-campaign-trump-charlie-kirk-1234947887/),” which spanned the U.S. in the leadup to the 2024 election. Part old-school revival, part campaign rally, the tour was an openly Christian nationalist crusade to elect Donald Trump.

TPUSA has not yet submitted its tax filing for the fiscal year ending June 30, 2024, but according to the tax filing from the [year before](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/800835023/202411369349309696/full) (ending nearly 18 months before the election), TPUSA Faith had become its own line item in the organization.

In that tax filing, TPUSA describes TPUSA Faith’s mission as:

_A movement to push back against secular totalitarianism in America, eradicate wokeism from the church, inspire the rise of strong churches, and wake up believers to their biblical responsibility to fight for freedom. TPUSA Faith equips Christians across the nation with the biblical, historical and constitutional knowledge they need to take a bold stand for liberty and God’s kingdom through TPUSA Faith courses, regional pastor roundtables, National Pastor’s Summits and Freedom Night in America events._

Expenses for TPUSA Faith ending June 30, 2023, totaled more than $13 million and the organization “coordinated” with 2,400 churches and 6,000 pastors attended its summits and roundtables targeting them.

[![Image 12](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/cefd985a2953f0e67777e6b9eae6b149998772563b5150f57b7367c386fc2420563ed4269bb0bdb5bc10bcc72673ba96f49ddc788d0c38afae0cabd0bb0d5f9c.jpeg?resize=278%2C278&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/cefd985a2953f0e67777e6b9eae6b149998772563b5150f57b7367c386fc2420563ed4269bb0bdb5bc10bcc72673ba96f49ddc788d0c38afae0cabd0bb0d5f9c.jpeg?ssl=1)There is an excellent new six-part documentary podcast called “[When the Wolves Came](https://www.ruthbraunstein.com/podcast)” that tracks how TPUSA Faith helped import Christian nationalism into churches on a massive scale.

TPUSA Faith has intertwined an extreme version of Christianity with the populist grievance-driven nationalist movement. Those who attend cannot differentiate between which elements of the TPUSA Faith events are worship service and which are political rally. The music, the lighting, the “sermons” and the calls to spiritual warfare on behalf of Trump bleed into calls to mobilize voters. And most of the events take place within the walls of actual churches, further blurring the boundary between what is Christianity and what is political extremism.

And that’s the point.

Charlie Kirk’s transformation is complete. He has gone from an angry white teenager being radicalized at racist Tea Party meetings to head of the most prolific organization radicalizing an entire generation of young people to the idolatry of Christian nationalism.

# How Charlie Kirk went from college dropout to Trump influencer

[Analysis](https://baptistnews.com/category/analysis/)[Mara Richards Bim](https://baptistnews.com/article/author/mrbim/)| April 15, 2025

![Image 4](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/AP24276792369838.jpg?resize=1200%2C500&ssl=1)

i

Donald Trump shakes hands with Turning Point CEO Charlie Kirk before speaking during the Turning Point USA Student Action Summit, Saturday, July 23, 2022, in Tampa, Fla. (AP Photo/Phelan M. Ebenhack)

_From BNG’s coverage earlier this year, first published April 15, 2025:_

**It seems Charlie Kirk — the Millennial founder** of the Christian nationalist powerhouse Turning Point USA — is everywhere these days.

He was part of a handful of Trump insiders tasked last fall with [administering](https://www.yahoo.com/news/charlie-kirk-conducting-loyalty-tests-184500064.html)[loyalty tests](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/12/07/us/politics/trump-administration-loyalty-test.html) to prospective hires for senior posts at the Pentagon and within the intelligence agencies.

More recently, Kirk, now 31, was one of a number of [loyalists](https://www.politico.com/news/2025/03/17/michael-flynn-charlie-kirk-trump-appointments-00234637) President Trump appointed to the boards of the military academies in the United States. Kirk was appointed to the Air Force Academy’s [Board of Visitors](https://www.usafa.edu/about/bov/) charged with inquiring into, among other things, the academy’s curriculum and instruction.

Kirk’s appointment is especially ironic. It was his [rejection](https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2022/10/20/charlie-kirks-republican-friends-00062305) from West Point Military Academy as a graduating senior in 2012 from Wheeling High School outside of Chicago that sent him on a downward spiral and into the arms of the burgeoning right-wing extremist movement which he now sits at the top of.

#### **The beginnings of Charlie Kirk**

In her book _Raising Them Right: The Untold Story of America’s Ultraconservative Youth Movement and its Plot for Power_, journalist Kyle Spencer sums up Kirk’s trajectory within the politics of resentment: “His metamorphosis can be seen as a case study of the power of grievance politics and a reminder that resentment is an energizing fuel most potent when delivered by leaders who have felt it deeply themselves.”

[![Image 5](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/i-went-to-high-school-with-charlie-kirk-v0-rclmfa50fhfc1.jpeg.jpg?resize=207%2C300&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/i-went-to-high-school-with-charlie-kirk-v0-rclmfa50fhfc1.jpeg.jpg?ssl=1)
Charlie Kirk as a high school senior

Kirk’s father was an architect with his own firm. He designed and built middle-class luxury estates while Kirk’s mother traded at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (she later went back to school to become a licensed therapist). Undoubtedly the 2008 housing crisis and the resulting bank bailouts impacted the Kirks’ businesses and was fodder for dinner table conversation in their five-bedroom mansion.

Kirk’s resentment was in full-bloom a few months later at the start of his freshman year under the new Obama presidency. Obama’s career began in the same Chicago suburb where Kirk attended high school. While the first African American president’s political win was celebrated by most in the rapidly diversifying suburb, it was not celebrated by Kirk.

Whether it was Obama’s continuance of George W. Bush’s bank bailouts or his skin color, Kirk was not a fan. In response, he began building a contrarian political persona around his freshman interpretation of Reagan economics, the work of the economist Milton Friedman and gun rights.

Kirk’s classmates described him as “rude,” “arrogant” and as someone with “a superiority complex.” He called teachers with whom he disagreed “neo-Marxists” and often was belligerent in class. On the topic of gun rights, Spencer [writes](https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2022/10/20/charlie-kirks-republican-friends-00062305) that Kirk “once asked a teacher if guns make people violent, ‘do forks make people fat?’”

By the time Kirk entered his senior year, the Tea Party was on the rise. Stanford sociologist Robb Willer conducted a [study](https://news.stanford.edu/stories/2016/05/perceived-threats-racial-status-drive-white-americans-support-tea-party-stanford-scholar-says) in 2016 that showed the rise of the Tea Party was directly linked to “the relative ‘racial standing’ of whites in the United States” with the election of Obama and the economic trends around 2008.

As a high school senior, Kirk began going to meetings and hanging out with right-wing political activists like 71-year old [Bill Montgomery](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/02/10/magazine/charlie-kirk-american-right.html) who, months later, would help Kirk co-found Turning Point USA. Also during his senior year, Kirk wrote an [opinion piece](https://dartreview.com/a-profile-of-charlie-kirk/) for the [controversial](https://bridge.georgetown.edu/research/factsheet-breitbart-news/)[misinformation](https://democracyforward.org/work/investigation-misinformation/) site Breitbart News, which landed him an interview on Fox News.

As he headed toward graduation, Kirk was denied entry into West Point — one of the most selective universities in America, with an [acceptance rate](https://www.prepscholar.com/sat/s/colleges/West-Point-admission-requirements#:~:text=The%20acceptance%20rate%20at%20West,and%20proving%20your%20academic%20preparation.) of 12%.

Kirk, however, [claimed](https://dartreview.com/a-profile-of-charlie-kirk/) his rejection was because he was passed over for “a far less-qualified candidate of a different gender and a different persuasion.”

[![Image 6](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/maxresdefault-43.jpg?resize=382%2C215&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/maxresdefault-43.jpg?ssl=1)
Social media post noting the death of Bill Montgomery.

Montgomery convinced him to take a gap year and work the political circuit. Using money he received for his high school graduation, Kirk launched TPUSA with Montgomery. He was 18 years old.

Kirk briefly attended[Harper College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harper_College), a community college near Chicago, but dropped out and never completed a degree.

#### **Politics of resentment**

In the fall of 2012 — just months after graduating high school — Kirk and TPUSA began by [sponsoring debates](https://www.newspapers.com/image/75778781) between Democratic and Republican students on a handful of college campuses in the Midwest. He also attended the Republican National Convention, where a chance meeting with multimillionaire investor Foster Freiss in a stairwell led to an infusion of cash into TPUSA.

After Obama won a second term in fall 2012, Kirk and TPUSA became integral to the infighting within the Republican Party. Kirk spent the next three years touring the country to speak at a variety of Republican — and primarily Tea Party — events. The Tea Party — having seen Republicans lose again in the 2012 presidential election — was livid and organizing. The target of their vitriol was the Affordable Care Act (which they dubbed “Obamacare”) and they were mobilizing to take over the Republican Party.

It was in these Tea Party meeting rooms that Kirk — a teenage, angry white male — learned to work a room and engage with political donors.

One such event was in June 2013 with then-Congressman Steve Daines (now senator), Montana’s then-Attorney General Tim Fox (who left office in [disgrace](https://flatheadbeacon.com/2020/12/23/what-an-embarrassment/) after signing onto a lawsuit challenging the 2020 election results) and former Montana Sen. Ryan Zinke (who later served as Trump’s first secretary of the interior and is now a representative for Montana).

[![Image 7](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/61369370.jpg?resize=245%2C375&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/61369370.jpg?ssl=1)Quoted afterward in _[The Montana Standard](https://www.newspapers.com/image/471013795),_ Kirk said he started TPUSA and was hanging out with right-wing Tea Party activists specifically because he was frustrated with the “too bureaucratic” Young Republicans who were unwilling to try new approaches to organizing.

By the time Donald J. Trump came onto the scene, Kirk had secured a spot within the remade Republican Party. More important, after marinating in resentment politics for several years, Kirk was a true believer.

Much has been written about Trump’s success at tapping into this grievance culture. Kirk, like many young white men who did not attend college, relished Trump’s offensive behavior and rhetoric. They felt “seen” again. And they began acting out and amplifying the behavior of their new leader.

#### **Charlie Kirk, Donald Trump and neo-Nazis**

On June 16, 2015, Trump made his [infamous descent](https://www.washingtonpost.com/video/politics/2015-trump-launches-presidential-campaign/2019/06/17/8e8d7747-e028-4f89-8e30-78d7311827e8_video.html) down the escalator at Trump Tower in New York City to officially launch his 2016 campaign. His inaugural speech was filled with the kind of [racist rhetoric](https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-election-trump/with-barbs-and-bluster-trump-barges-into-2016-white-house-race-idUSKBN0OW1ZU20150618/) he had become known for after five years of [falsely](https://www.wsj.com/articles/BL-WB-65498) saying Barack Obama was not born in America.

The next day, a 21-year old white supremacist neo-Nazi attended a Bible study at Mother Emanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church in Charleston, S.C. At the end of the study, he stood up and [opened fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charleston_church_shooting) on the 10 African American church members who had opened their community to him — killing nine of them, including the senior pastor, state senator Clementa C. Pinckney.

These events — Trump’s racist campaign, the mass shooting at a historic African American church and the platforming of a young, angry white Charlie Kirk — are in many ways the starting point for where we are in today’s political landscape filled with conspiracy theories and the rise of Christian nationalism.

Weeks after the Mother Emanuel shootings, Kirk joined the Trump campaign, where he became friends with the future president’s son, Donald Trump Jr. He also launched Turning Point Action Inc., a 501(c)(4) tied to his nonprofit TPUSA. The new nonprofit strategically placed him within the [web of dark money](https://baptistnews.com/article/want-to-know-whos-behind-project-2025-follow-the-money-through-the-swamp/) that [continues](https://baptistnews.com/article/following-leonard-leos-dark-money-in-pushing-america-to-the-far-right/) to this day.

[![Image 8](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/06/ezgif.com-gif-maker-70.jpg?resize=300%2C280&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/06/ezgif.com-gif-maker-70.jpg?ssl=1)
Charlie Kirk with Jerry Falwell Jr. in a publicity photo for the Falkirk Center at Liberty University. The name was a mash up for Falwell and Kirk.

After Trump’s surprise victory in 2016, Kirk and TPUSA upped the ante on their provocative antics by publishing a “[Professor Watchlist](https://www.newspapers.com/image/656391804/).” The list targeted college professors who [Kirk accused](https://www.newspapers.com/image/364943350/) (without evidence) of promoting undefined “leftist propaganda.”

Individuals from across the political spectrum decried the move and called it a “[witch hunt](https://www.newspapers.com/image/1077717863/)” and [reminiscent](https://www.newspapers.com/image/693557361/) of Sen. Joseph McCarthy’s [political persecution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCarthyism) of anyone he thought might be a communist.

This list was just TPUSA’s opening salvo in an escalating war on college campuses; but the war on college campuses wasn’t the only war raging in the early days of the Trump presidency. In the aftermath of the Mother Emanuel mass shooting and anti-Black hate crime, calls echoed across the South to once and for all [remove the monuments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Removal_of_Confederate_monuments_and_memorials) erected to memorialize the Confederacy from the Civil War.

These [monuments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederate_monuments_and_memorials) — raised up during and after the height of Jim Crow laws — continued to feed the [Lost Cause](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lost_Cause_of_the_Confederacy) narrative embraced by white supremacists. That [myth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lost_Cause_of_the_Confederacy) — that the heroic Confederacy rose up to justly fight the Civil War as an act of liberty rather than over slavery — has influenced every facet of life in the South since it was first deployed in 1866.

In the first year of Trump’s presidency, fueled in no small part by the president’s continued racist rhetoric, battles over Confederate monuments reached a fevered pitch.

On Aug. 11, 2017, after weeks of [publicizing](https://www.nytimes.com/2018/08/12/us/politics/charlottesville-va-protest-unite-the-right.html) it, white supremacist and neo-Nazi groups descended on the streets of [Charlottesville, Va.,](https://time.com/charlottesville-white-nationalist-rally-clashes/) under the [pretense](https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/archive/2017/08/nazis-racism-charlottesville/536928/) of protesting the removal of a statue of Robert E. Lee. Angry white men marched through the streets carrying tiki torches and shouting slogans like “Jews will not replace us.”

While young, angry white supremacist neo-Nazis were taking to the streets in cities like Charlottesville, they were beginning to take note of Kirk and TPUSA.

After releasing the “Professor Watchlist,” Kirk and TPUSA began [booking appearances](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2017/jan/28/milo-yiannopoulos-campus-speaking-tour-colorado) with alt-right neo-Nazis like Milo Yiannopoulos. These campus appearances led to massive (and [sometimes violent](https://www.cnn.com/2017/02/01/us/milo-yiannopoulos-berkeley/index.html)) protests on college campuses.

After Charlottesville, white supremacists and neo-Nazis flocked to TPUSA events on college campuses and elsewhere, looking to fight with counter protesters. Kirk did [nothing](https://truthout.org/articles/young-fascists-on-campus-turning-point-usa-and-its-far-right-connections/) to separate himself or TPUSA from them.

> “After Charlottesville, white supremacists and neo-Nazis flocked to TPUSA events on college campuses.”

In fact, many of TPUSA’s field organizers embraced the white supremacists in their midst. So much so that the media started taking note. Rather than distancing itself from racists and neo-Nazis, Kirk and TPUSA began offering “new and former staff with complimentary [social media background checks](https://www.huffpost.com/entry/turning-point-usa-racist-tweets_n_5ad65b06e4b029ebe01ed1ac)” to uncover past racist behavior “that could potentially damage your credibility or the credibility of the organization.”

TPUSA had become a powerhouse in national politics and Kirk didn’t want to see the organization brought down by inconvenient ties to racism.

For example, during the 2018 midterms, Turning Point Action Inc. and TPUSA both engaged the marketing firm Rally Forge to place ads from a fake liberal organization and to create a troll farm on Facebook to [promote Republican candidates](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2021/jun/11/facebook-ads-turning-point-usa-rally-forge). From July 2018 to June 2019, the two organizations paid Rally Forge nearly $1 million for the ads.

[![Image 9](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/52147677176_f76c3a7f46_o.jpg?resize=1700%2C1040&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/52147677176_f76c3a7f46_o.jpg?ssl=1)
Charlie Kirk speaks to a gathering sponsored by the Conservative Baptist Network during the SBC annual meeting.

#### **Kirk embraces Christian nationalism**

In the years between Trump’s 2020 election defeat and his 2024 campaign, Kirk found himself at odds with neo-Nazi groups. To their mind, TPUSA wasn’t [racist enough](https://www.dailydot.com/debug/charlie-kirk-white-nationalist-nick-fuentes-turning-point-usa/). That didn’t keep Kirk or TPUSA from [schmoozing with them](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/nazis-mingle-openly-cpac-spreading-antisemitic-conspiracy-theories-fin-rcna140335) at events like the Conservative Political Action Conference. Nevertheless, Kirk and TPUSA sought to distance themselves publicly from neo-Nazism. As they did, they moved toward a full-throated embrace of [Christian nationalism](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2024-election/charlie-kirk-turning-point-donald-trump-christian-nationalism-rcna156565).

Recently, there have been several [articles](https://www.rollingstone.com/politics/politics-features/charlie-kirk-turning-point-usa-pivots-to-christian-nationalism-1234740083/) noting the [evolution](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2024-election/charlie-kirk-turning-point-donald-trump-christian-nationalism-rcna156565) of Kirk and TPUSA from an organization devoted to promoting free market capitalism to one focused on promoting Christian nationalism.

In 2018, during an [interview](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FhCKfxy83BQ&t=166s) titled “Defending Christianity and Discussing Radical Islam,” Kirk told conservative commentator Dave Rubin Christians should respect the separation of church and state. But in 2022, Kirk — in his own podcast — [declared](https://www.mediamatters.org/charlie-kirk/charlie-kirk-there-no-separation-church-and-state): “There is no separation of church and state. It’s a fabrication. It’s a fiction. It’s not in the Constitution. It’s made up by secular humanists. It’s derived from a single letter that Thomas Jefferson wrote to the Danbury Baptist Convention.”

This assertion is a nearly word-for-word talking point from the controversial pseudo-historian [David Barton](https://www.texastribune.org/2022/07/29/texas-church-state-separation-opposition/).

[![Image 10](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/AP24167249757668.jpg?resize=300%2C200&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/AP24167249757668.jpg?ssl=1)
An attendee shows off his copy of Right Wing Revolution by Charlie Kirk at The People’s Convention hosted by Turning Point USA in Detroit on June 14, 2024. (Photo by Adam J. Dewey/NurPhoto via AP)

On TPUSA’s 2021 tax filing, TPUSA [redefined its mission](https://apps.irs.gov/pub/epostcard/cor/800835023_202206_990_2023060921420938.pdf) for the first time since its founding. Now, just months after the January 6 attempted insurrection, TPUSA was no longer focused on “fiscal responsibility, free markets and capitalism through non-partisan debate, dialogue and discussion.” Instead, TPUSA identified its mission as:

_To empower informed civic and cultural engagement grounded in American Exceptionalism and a positive spirit of action. Turning Point USA guides citizens through development of knowledge, skills, values and motivation, so they can meaningfully engage in their communities to restore traditional American values like patriotism, respect for life, liberty, family and fiscal responsibility._

The 2021 tax filing also is the first one in which TPUSA listed as one of its programs “TPUSA Faith.” TPUSA received a $50,000 gift in the early part of 2022 from [It Takes a Family Foundation](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/582276414) — a right-wing, NAR-supporting family foundation that also funds the extremist groups Family Research Council, Project Veritas, Judicial Watch, Sean Feucht’s Let Us Worship and Barton’s Wallbuilders, among others.

[![Image 11](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/CouragerTour.jpg?resize=2200%2C916&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/CouragerTour.jpg?ssl=1)
Screenshot from Courage Tour website

In fact, it seems the family members behind It Takes a Family Foundation are the connection between Kirk’s TPUSA, Sean Feucht’s ministry and NAR frontman Lance Wallnau. Together, these three men created “[The Courage Tour](https://www.rollingstone.com/politics/politics-features/christian-nationalists-churches-campaign-trump-charlie-kirk-1234947887/),” which spanned the U.S. in the leadup to the 2024 election. Part old-school revival, part campaign rally, the tour was an openly Christian nationalist crusade to elect Donald Trump.

TPUSA has not yet submitted its tax filing for the fiscal year ending June 30, 2024, but according to the tax filing from the [year before](https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/800835023/202411369349309696/full) (ending nearly 18 months before the election), TPUSA Faith had become its own line item in the organization.

In that tax filing, TPUSA describes TPUSA Faith’s mission as:

_A movement to push back against secular totalitarianism in America, eradicate wokeism from the church, inspire the rise of strong churches, and wake up believers to their biblical responsibility to fight for freedom. TPUSA Faith equips Christians across the nation with the biblical, historical and constitutional knowledge they need to take a bold stand for liberty and God’s kingdom through TPUSA Faith courses, regional pastor roundtables, National Pastor’s Summits and Freedom Night in America events._

Expenses for TPUSA Faith ending June 30, 2023, totaled more than $13 million and the organization “coordinated” with 2,400 churches and 6,000 pastors attended its summits and roundtables targeting them.

[![Image 12](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/cefd985a2953f0e67777e6b9eae6b149998772563b5150f57b7367c386fc2420563ed4269bb0bdb5bc10bcc72673ba96f49ddc788d0c38afae0cabd0bb0d5f9c.jpeg?resize=278%2C278&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/baptistnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/cefd985a2953f0e67777e6b9eae6b149998772563b5150f57b7367c386fc2420563ed4269bb0bdb5bc10bcc72673ba96f49ddc788d0c38afae0cabd0bb0d5f9c.jpeg?ssl=1)There is an excellent new six-part documentary podcast called “[When the Wolves Came](https://www.ruthbraunstein.com/podcast)” that tracks how TPUSA Faith helped import Christian nationalism into churches on a massive scale.

TPUSA Faith has intertwined an extreme version of Christianity with the populist grievance-driven nationalist movement. Those who attend cannot differentiate between which elements of the TPUSA Faith events are worship service and which are political rally. The music, the lighting, the “sermons” and the calls to spiritual warfare on behalf of Trump bleed into calls to mobilize voters. And most of the events take place within the walls of actual churches, further blurring the boundary between what is Christianity and what is political extremism.

And that’s the point.

Charlie Kirk’s transformation is complete. He has gone from an angry white teenager being radicalized at racist Tea Party meetings to head of the most prolific organization radicalizing an entire generation of young people to the idolatry of Christian nationalism.

As someone who's: Dropped out of college (twice), Traveled and worked across Europe and the U.S., Helped drag entire government systems online as a network admin and IT project manager (back when that still involved yelling "YES IT'S PLUGGED IN" into a desk phone), Survived Y2K (yes, in a server room waiting for the apocalypse), Founded a cybersecurity startup that crashed and burned after the post-9/11 crash, Finished my BS because "0 degree" was holding me back. Earned an MBA, because apparently experience wasn't enough either, Taught myself to code, because degrees weren't enough, Got certified, because coding wasn't enough, And now? Advised to downplay it all so I don't "age out" of the hiring pool... … I'm watching this dropout trend with the same energy I had when someone pitched a startup that replaces email with AI-powered carrier pigeons. I've done the dropout path. I've done the degree path. I've done the bootstrap, retrain, rebrand, and "please ignore my birthday" path. At this point? I don't care if you're a dropout or a double PhD. If you can build, lead, adapt, and not melt under pressure — you're already ahead of the game. Here's to 2026: May it be the year we stop judging founders by where they left and start looking at where they've actually been. 🧠 Skills > Signals 🛠️ Experience > Aesthetics 👀 Results > Rhetoric 📆 And yes — Age ≠ Irrelevance Happy New Year. Especially to my fellow "overqualified" misfits who never fit the mold — but somehow kept building anyway. Is college necessary? Dropping out is in style again. Apparently, Sam Altman envies 20-year-old dropouts with unlimited headspace. More than anything else, college teaches structured thinking, persistence, hard work, and 𝐝𝐞𝐥𝐚𝐲𝐞𝐝 𝐠𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧. All extremely valuable for the 99.9% of young adults who are not already at that level. 𝐁𝐲 𝐦𝐚𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐞𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐣𝐨𝐛𝐬 𝐬𝐜𝐚𝐫𝐜𝐞, 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐔𝐒 𝐠𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐡𝐞𝐥𝐩𝐢𝐧𝐠. College dropouts like Gates, Jobs, and Zuckerberg get the headlines. But they're the exceptions, not the norm. What strikes me about Altman's comments is the assumption that innovation requires complete freedom from structure. Often true, but those who don't know how to execute with structure won't get far from idea to success. A LinkedIn survey showing only 41% of junior professionals believe degrees are essential reflects a dangerous oversimplification. Yes, AI democratizes creation. But building sustainable businesses still requires the foundational skills that good education provides. The real question isn't whether to drop out. It's how we 𝐦𝐚𝐤𝐞 𝐞𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐥𝐞𝐯𝐚𝐧𝐭 to rapid technological change while preserving its core value in developing critical thinking. Dropping out of college is not an achievement. I saw this a lot at YC and we've even gotten a couple resumes that are proud of being college dropouts. But if you drop out of college, you should be doing something more exceptional with your time. That's the achievement, not the fact that you're dropping out. My brother/cofounder Brett is a college dropout, and I would have been too if my dad hadn't pushed me so hard to finish. But Brett dropped out specifically because he already had a high paying job at [Podium](https://www.linkedin.com/company/podium?trk=news_storyline_guest-text). I wanted to drop out specifically to pursue a startup. I don't think college is the right move for a lot of people, but don't drop out if you don't have plans for something better. Dropping out just to drop out is not something to celebrate.

TechCrunch says that leaving college (or high school… or kindergarten, I assume) is now the new badge of honor in startup land. As someone who's: Dropped out of college (twice), Traveled and worked across Europe and the U.S., Helped drag entire government systems online as a network admin and IT project manager (back when that still involved yelling "YES IT'S PLUGGED IN" into a desk phone), Survived Y2K (yes, in a server room waiting for the apocalypse), Founded a cybersecurity startup that crashed and burned after the post-9/11 crash, Finished my BS because "0 degree" was holding me back. I've done the dropout path. I've done the degree path. I've done the bootstrap, retrain, rebrand, and "please ignore my birthday" path. At this point? I don't care if you're a dropout or a double PhD. If you can build, lead, adapt, and not melt under pressure — you're already ahead of the game. Here's to 2026: May it be the year we stop judging founders by where they left and start looking at where they've actually been. 🧠 Skills > Signals 🛠️ Experience > Aesthetics 👀 Results > Rhetoric 📆 And yes — Age ≠ Irrelevance Happy New Year. Is college necessary? Dropping out is in style again. Apparently, Sam Altman envies 20-year-old dropouts with unlimited headspace. More than anything else, college teaches structured thinking, persistence, hard work, and 𝐝𝐞𝐥𝐚𝐲𝐞𝐝 𝐠𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧. All extremely valuable for the 99.9% of young adults who are not already at that level. 𝐁𝐲 𝐦𝐚𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐞𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐣𝐨𝐛𝐬 𝐬𝐜𝐚𝐫𝐜𝐞, 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐔𝐒 𝐠𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐡𝐞𝐥𝐩𝐢𝐧𝐠. College dropouts like Gates, Jobs, and Zuckerberg get the headlines. But they're the exceptions, not the norm. What strikes me about Altman's comments is the assumption that innovation requires complete freedom from structure. Often true, but those who don't know how to execute with structure won't get far from idea to success. A LinkedIn survey showing only 41% of junior professionals believe degrees are essential reflects a dangerous oversimplification. Yes, AI democratizes creation. But building sustainable businesses still requires the foundational skills that good education provides. The real question isn't whether to drop out. It's how we 𝐦𝐚𝐤𝐞 𝐞𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐥𝐞𝐯𝐚𝐧𝐭 to rapid technological change while preserving its core value in developing critical thinking. **Dropout** is an American comedy [subscription streaming service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_on_demand "Video on demand") run by the production company of the same name (formerly [CollegeHumor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CollegeHumor "CollegeHumor")), founded in September 2018. Its ad-free original shows are mainly composed of [live play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_play "Live play"), such as _[Dimension 20](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension\_20 "Dimension 20")_ hosted by [Brennan Lee Mulligan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brennan_Lee_Mulligan "Brennan Lee Mulligan"), and [improv comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Improv_comedy "Improv comedy") and [panel shows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panel_show "Panel show") like _[Game Changer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game\_Changer\_(game\_show) "Game Changer (game show)")_ and its spinoff _[Make Some Noise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Make\_Some\_Noise\_(TV\_series) "Make Some Noise (TV series)")_, both hosted by Dropout owner and CEO [Sam Reich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Reich "Sam Reich"), and _[Very Important People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Very\_Important\_People\_(2023\_TV\_series) "Very Important People (2023 TV series)")_ hosted by [Vic Michaelis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vic_Michaelis "Vic Michaelis"). Dropout's series often feature a rotating cast of regular comedians and performers.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dropout_(streaming_service)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### CollegeHumor

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dropout_(streaming_service)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: CollegeHumor")]

Main article: [CollegeHumor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CollegeHumor "CollegeHumor")

Originally founded in 1999 by [Josh Abramson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josh_Abramson "Josh Abramson") and [Ricky Van Veen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricky_Van_Veen "Ricky Van Veen"), then-independent website CollegeHumor was acquired by holding media and entertainment company [IAC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAC_Inc. "IAC Inc.") in August 2006.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-1) CollegeHumor's work originally only included editorial articles, but eventually expanded to include online video and development and production of TV shows.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Digiday_-_lost_its_early-2) In 2013, the video production CollegeHumor team moved to Los Angeles to continue to create online and traditional video consisting of shows like _[Adam Ruins Everything](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam\_Ruins\_Everything "Adam Ruins Everything")_ and _[Hot Date](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot\_Date "Hot Date")_ as well as sketch and short-form comedy on its [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube "YouTube") channel.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Digiday_-_lost_its_early-2) However, ad revenue became increasingly scarce, with YouTube's unfavorable ad rates and an ongoing risk of CollegeHumor's content being demonetized on the platform, as well as Facebook's inflated viewership numbers not bringing in anticipated ad sales.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Knibbs_Wired-3)

In the mid-2010s, CollegeHumor syndicated its content to various companies, including [Condé Nast Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cond%C3%A9_Nast_Entertainment "Condé Nast Entertainment"), [DailyMotion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DailyMotion "DailyMotion"), Samsung, [Vessel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vessel_(website) "Vessel (website)"), and Watchable.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-var-roettgers-15-4) CollegeHumor subsidiary Big Breakfast signed a deal with Verizon's [go90](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Go90 "Go90") streaming service in 2015, which included the show _Fatal Decision_ and a commitment of ten video clips per month for the platform.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-var-roettgers-15-4) During this time, Shane Rahmani served as CollegeHumor's general manager. _Fatal Decision_ was ultimately released on Dropout's own platform in 2025.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-var-roettgers-15-4)

After starting production in 2017, CollegeHumor launched its Dropout TV video platform on September 26, 2018.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Anthony_Ha_TechCrunch-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-fast-company-interview-24-8) CollegeHumor's then-CEO, Rich Cusick, announced the service as a "TV-MA version of CollegeHumor" that would "allow us to double down our investment into premium original content, resulting in a bigger, better, badder CollegeHumor."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Max_Godnick_Cheddar-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Todd_Spangler_Variety-10) Dropout was also pitched as a way to allow fans to dive deeper into pre-established popular characters and shows from CollegeHumor's YouTube channel.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Max_Godnick_Cheddar-9) CollegeHumor's Chief Creative Officer, [Sam Reich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Reich "Sam Reich"), also claimed that the founding of Dropout was in response to difficulty in receiving advertising dollars on traditional media platforms for mature content.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-11) At launch, Dropout announced a mix of scripted and unscripted content, as well as digital comics and chat-story content and a subscriber-only Discord.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Todd_Spangler_Variety-10)

Dropout utilizes CollegeHumor spinoff [Vimeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vimeo "Vimeo") as its hosting service.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-12) Dropout officially launched native [iOS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IOS "IOS") and [Android](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Android_(operating_system) "Android (operating system)") apps for its service in December 2018, allowing users to watch shows and also cast to smart TVs. Comics and chat stories were also integrated into the app.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-NativeApp-13)

### Independent ownership

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dropout_(streaming_service)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Independent ownership")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/Samreich.jpg/250px-Samreich.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Samreich.jpg)

Dropout CEO [Sam Reich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Reich "Sam Reich") (pictured in 2024) acquired a majority interest in the service in 2020.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-iac-ha-20-14)

After launch, Dropout saw that the unscripted and less expensive content both acquired and retained viewers, while more expensive and scripted shows neither acquired nor retained viewers, with the limited exception of _WTF 101_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Digiday_-_lost_its_early-2)_[Dimension 20](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension\_20 "Dimension 20")_ became the most popular show on the platform, followed by _Um, Actually_ and _Cartoon Hell_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Digiday_-_lost_its_early-2)_[Game Changer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game\_Changer\_(game\_show) "Game Changer (game show)")_, hosted by Reich, would also become a success upon launch in 2019.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Digiday_-_lost_its_early-2) A year after Dropout's launch, the service had between 75,000 and 100,000 subscribers.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Bethy_Squires_Vulture-15) Dropout planned to release a new original title per month in 2019, according to Sam Reich.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Todd_Spangler_Variety-10)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-16) However, the programming slate did not allow Dropout to pivot quickly enough away from scripted content and it was still not profitable by the end of 2019; Reich later noted that "we had a writer's room full of scripted comedy writers. All of us were sort of having to pivot to think about something that wasn't our primary skill set."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-dead-june-12-24-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Peter_Kafka_Recode-18) Because Dropout was in the middle of a $30 million subscription investment, the streamer was on track to "lose" another $10 million by the end of 2019 before it would be profitable.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Peter_Kafka_Recode-18)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Digiday_-_lost_its_early-2)

In January 2020, IAC announced it had ceased financing CollegeHumor, leading to the layoff of 105 employees.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Anthony_Ha_TechCrunch-5)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Bethy_Squires_Vulture-15)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-vulture-like-2009-19) IAC unsuccessfully attempted to sell CollegeHumor to numerous studios and entertainment companies at this time, reportedly seeking up to $100 million for the company;[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-fast-company-interview-24-8)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-20)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Peter_Kafka_Recode-18)[Viacom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount_Global "Paramount Global") offered to buy CollegeHumor and its back catalog for $3 million.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-vulture-like-2009-19) IAC ultimately sold CollegeHumor to Reich, the then-Chief Creative Officer, in 2020, who transitioned to CEO as a result.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-iac-ha-20-14) IAC kept a minority stake in Dropout,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Anthony_Ha_TechCrunch-5) having been convinced by Reich it had the potential to become worth more than Viacom's offer.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-vulture-like-2009-19) The deal was finalized in March 2020.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-fast-company-interview-24-8) Dropout ended production on scripted shows and focused on unscripted shows such as _Um, Actually_, _[Dimension 20](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension\_20 "Dimension 20")_, and _[Game Changer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game\_Changer\_(game\_show) "Game Changer (game show)")_, briefly producing these series through online conference during the beginning of the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

During the July-November [2023 SAG-AFTRA strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_SAG-AFTRA_strike "2023 SAG-AFTRA strike"), Dropout series such as _Dimension 20_, _Game Changer_ and _Um, Actually_ were initially shut down.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Gizmodo_Strike-21) Reich stated:

> Because we aren't associated with the [AMPTP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AMPTP "AMPTP"), it's possible we may be able to reach an interim agreement with [SAG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SAG-AFTRA "SAG-AFTRA") that allows us to continue to produce content during the strike. But we'll only do that, obviously, if we get the blessing of the union and the buy-in of our performers. If not, we have enough content in the can to last us a little past the end of the year.... As for me, I intend to honor my union's position that I not promote SAG productions as a performer – even if they are produced by me. That means that I won't personally be promoting any of our shows for the time being.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-22)

In August 2023, Reich announced that all Dropout shows had resumed production as it was determined that their "New Media Agreement for Non-Dramatic Programming" was actually a non-struck SAG-AFTRA contract.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Dropout_August_2023_Update-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-var-maas-23-25)

Also in August 2023, [NPR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NPR "NPR") stated that "Dropout has not shared their official subscriber count, but Reich says it's in the mid-hundreds of thousands. He's very aware that doesn't come close to the hundreds of millions of subscribers that large media companies have, but, to him, that's not necessarily a problem.... Though they're not required to by unions, he said Dropout is working to become one of the first streamers to pay [residuals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Residual_(entertainment_industry) "Residual (entertainment industry)") to their writers, actors, and crew members".[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-26) Dropout also pays performers to audition.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-fast-company-interview-24-8) Dropout's overall subscriber count almost doubled during 2023;[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-var-maas-23-25) By October 2025, Dropout had over a million subscribers.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-LATimes2025-27)

Dropout officially retired all CollegeHumor branding in September 2023.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-poly-polo-23-28) Later that year, Dropout [shared its profit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Profit_sharing "Profit sharing") with its employees and other workers,[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-esq-sg-24-29)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-var-maas-23-25)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-fast-company-interview-24-8) giving them between a tenth and a fourth of their total earnings.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-vulture-like-2009-19) This practice continued in 2024 for a second year. Additionally, Dropout offers higher-than-average pay to performers: due to its heavy use of prosthetics, actors on _[Very Important People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Very\_Important\_People\_(2023\_TV\_series) "Very Important People (2023 TV series)")_ are paid between $5,000 and $10,000 per episode, and main cast members of _[Dimension 20](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension\_20 "Dimension 20")_ are paid approximately $7,000 per episode.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-vulture-like-2009-19) Stand-up comedian [Gianmarco Soresi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gianmarco_Soresi "Gianmarco Soresi") made more money filming one episode of _[Game Changer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game\_Changer\_(game\_show) "Game Changer (game show)")_ than he did for his role on the [Paramount+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount+ "Paramount+") show _Crutch_.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-vulture-like-2009-19) Reich himself earned almost nothing during the first two years of Dropout ownership; in 2022 he earned over $1 million.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-vulture-like-2009-19)

Dropout signed an expansion deal with [talent agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talent_agency "Talent agency")[CAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creative_Artists_Agency "Creative Artists Agency") in July 2025.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-dead-grobar-25-30) In August 2025, _[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety\_(magazine) "Variety (magazine)")_ reported that [Brennan Lee Mulligan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brennan_Lee_Mulligan "Brennan Lee Mulligan") had "struck a new three-year development deal at his longtime home media company Dropout".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Variety-2025-31) In the 10th episode of _[Game Changer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game\_Changer\_(game\_show) "Game Changer (game show)")_'s seventh season, [Vic Michaelis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vic_Michaelis "Vic Michaelis") and [Aabria Iyengar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aabria_Iyengar "Aabria Iyengar") were elected as [honorary presidents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honorary_President "Honorary President") of Dropout.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-33)

## Production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dropout_(streaming_service)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Production")]

Dropout is headquartered in [Silver Lake, Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_Lake,_Los_Angeles "Silver Lake, Los Angeles"). The company's production studio includes two sound stages, one for _Dimension 20_ and one which rotates between other productions, as well as an art studio for set and prop design. As of 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dropout_(streaming_service)&action=edit), the company has 40 full-time employees.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-LATimes2025-27)

## Service and availability

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dropout_(streaming_service)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Service and availability")]

Dropout is available worldwide; as of 2024[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dropout_(streaming_service)&action=edit) around 60% of subscribers were in the United States.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-esq-sg-24-29)

### Subscription model

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dropout_(streaming_service)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Subscription model")]

The company has justified the pricing model as allowing them to create content without being dependent on, or beholden to, requests from advertisers.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-34) In December 2018, visitors to the service spent on average 31 minutes per visit, and visited on average 3.5 times per week.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-NativeApp-13) Throughout 2019, Dropout began to experiment with more live streaming versions of their shows, through using [Twitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitch_(service) "Twitch (service)") and podcast-like formats. At the end of 2023, the average user subscribed for 18 months; Reich said in June 2024 that the statistic is continuing to increase.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-var-maas-23-25)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-fast-company-interview-24-8)As of June 2024[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dropout_(streaming_service)&action=edit), Dropout earns around 80–85% of its revenue via subscriptions.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-fast-company-interview-24-8)

Dropout launched with a beta price of $3.99 per month for the first three months of the service. After December 2018, the price rose to a three tiered option, with monthly memberships for $5.99/month, semi-annual memberships for $4.99/month, and annual memberships for $3.99/month.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-35)As of January 2022[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dropout_(streaming_service)&action=edit), new subscribers paid $5.99 monthly or $59.99 yearly, while those who already subscribed prior to that date were charged $4.99 monthly or $47.99 yearly.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Dec_2021_tweet-36) In April 2025, Dropout announced a subscription cost increase ($6.99 monthly or $69.99 annually) which took effect on May 7, 2025. However, this increase did not impact existing subscribers who were [grandfathered in](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandfathered_in "Grandfathered in") to the legacy subscription cost.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-38)

In August 2019, CollegeHumor partnered with [Facebook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facebook "Facebook") to offer Dropout content via paid video subscriptions on Facebook's platform.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-39) Users are also able to access Dropout content through YouTube via the join function.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In October 2025, CEO Sam Reich announced a "Superfan" subscription for $129.99 a year, described as a 'Pay more if you feel like it' tier. Perks include behind the scenes content, discounts and additional items in Dropout's online store, and early access to purchase tickets for live events.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-40)

### Services

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dropout_(streaming_service)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Services")]

In addition to original series, Dropout offered videos produced by CollegeHumor 72 hours before they were released to the public. Previously, a subscriber-only [Discord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discord_(software) "Discord (software)") server was included as a service, later expanded to non-subscribers as well, until its closure on May 26, 2024. Dropout also has a store which sells merchandise (such as shirts, stickers, and mugs) related to shows on the platform.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-41)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-42)

In February 2026, Dropout announced that British surrealist [adult puppet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adult_puppeteering "Adult puppeteering") musical [comedy horror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_horror "Comedy horror") web series _[Don't Hug Me I'm Scared](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don't\_Hug\_Me\_I'm\_Scared "Don't Hug Me I'm Scared")_ would be non-exclusively licensed to them for three years, in the first-ever licensing deal for Dropout.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-43)
