## Original shows

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dropout_(streaming_service)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Original shows")]

See also: [CollegeHumor §List of CH Originals series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CollegeHumor#List_of_CH_Originals_series "CollegeHumor")

Shows on Dropout are usually released [fortnightly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortnight "Fortnight"), a schedule used more often for podcasts than for television.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-var-maas-23-25) Dropout planned to release a new original title per month in 2019, according to Sam Reich.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Todd_Spangler_Variety-10)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-54) By 2020, the service had retired all scripted shows in favor of cheaper and more successful unscripted content.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-poly-polo-23-28)

_Dirty Laundry_, _Play It By Ear_, and _[Make Some Noise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Make\_Some\_Noise\_(TV\_series) "Make Some Noise (TV series)")_, each spun off from _Game Changer_, premiered throughout 2022. In 2023, Dropout started airing the improvisational interview show _[Very Important People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Very\_Important\_People\_(2023\_TV\_series) "Very Important People (2023 TV series)")_, and in 2024 six new shows premiered: _Smartypants_, _Thousandaires_, _Dropout Presents_, _Monét's Slumber Party_, _Gastronauts_, and _Nobody Asked_.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-npr-luse-24-55)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-ta-champagne-24-56)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-brown-int-yt-24-57)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-var-maas-monet-24-49)

A show called _Parlor Room_, hosted by Becca Scott, was announced in March 2025 and premiered on April 18, 2025.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-pr-sheehan-25-58) A fourth _Game Changer_ spinoff, _Crowd Control_, premiered on September 8, 2025.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-vulture-like-2009-19)

As of October 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dropout_(streaming_service)&action=edit), an untitled animated show was in development.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-LATimes2025-27) A livestream channel titled _Dropout 24/7_, which airs Dropout shows continuously, launched on February 18, 2026; this channel is exclusive to the Dropout platform. The channel began with a [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_(media) "Marathon (media)") of _Dimension 20_.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-59)

### Dropout Improv

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dropout_(streaming_service)&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Dropout Improv")]

Dropout Improv is an [improvisational comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Improvisational_comedy "Improvisational comedy") tour featuring regular Dropout performers, it has toured both North America and the United Kingdom.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-var-maas-di-25-115)

A panel event called "Cue the Chaos: In Convo with Dropout Improv" took place at the [Just for Laughs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just_for_Laughs "Just for Laughs") comedy festival in [Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal "Montreal") on July 26, 2025.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-jpr-25-116) Sam Reich also appeared at a "fireside chat" on July 24 as one of the festival's more exclusive "ComedyPRO" events.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-reich-jfl-25-117)

Dates for a Dropout Improv tour in [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia") and [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand "New Zealand") are scheduled in 2026 for [Perth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perth "Perth"), [Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney "Sydney"), [Melbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne "Melbourne"), and [Auckland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland "Auckland").[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-aur-santos-25-118)

**Dropout** is an American comedy [subscription streaming service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_on_demand "Video on demand") run by the production company of the same name (formerly [CollegeHumor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CollegeHumor "CollegeHumor")), founded in September 2018. Its ad-free original shows are mainly composed of [live play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_play "Live play"), such as _[Dimension 20](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension\_20 "Dimension 20")_ hosted by [Brennan Lee Mulligan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brennan_Lee_Mulligan "Brennan Lee Mulligan"), and [improv comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Improv_comedy "Improv comedy") and [panel shows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panel_show "Panel show") like _[Game Changer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game\_Changer\_(game\_show) "Game Changer (game show)")_ and its spinoff _[Make Some Noise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Make\_Some\_Noise\_(TV\_series) "Make Some Noise (TV series)")_, both hosted by Dropout owner and CEO [Sam Reich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Reich "Sam Reich"), and _[Very Important People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Very\_Important\_People\_(2023\_TV\_series) "Very Important People (2023 TV series)")_ hosted by [Vic Michaelis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vic_Michaelis "Vic Michaelis"). Dropout's series often feature a rotating cast of regular comedians and performers.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dropout_(streaming_service)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### CollegeHumor

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dropout_(streaming_service)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: CollegeHumor")]

Main article: [CollegeHumor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CollegeHumor "CollegeHumor")

Originally founded in 1999 by [Josh Abramson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josh_Abramson "Josh Abramson") and [Ricky Van Veen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricky_Van_Veen "Ricky Van Veen"), then-independent website CollegeHumor was acquired by holding media and entertainment company [IAC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAC_Inc. "IAC Inc.") in August 2006.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-1) CollegeHumor's work originally only included editorial articles, but eventually expanded to include online video and development and production of TV shows.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Digiday_-_lost_its_early-2) In 2013, the video production CollegeHumor team moved to Los Angeles to continue to create online and traditional video consisting of shows like _[Adam Ruins Everything](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam\_Ruins\_Everything "Adam Ruins Everything")_ and _[Hot Date](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot\_Date "Hot Date")_ as well as sketch and short-form comedy on its [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube "YouTube") channel.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Digiday_-_lost_its_early-2) However, ad revenue became increasingly scarce, with YouTube's unfavorable ad rates and an ongoing risk of CollegeHumor's content being demonetized on the platform, as well as Facebook's inflated viewership numbers not bringing in anticipated ad sales.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Knibbs_Wired-3)

In the mid-2010s, CollegeHumor syndicated its content to various companies, including [Condé Nast Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cond%C3%A9_Nast_Entertainment "Condé Nast Entertainment"), [DailyMotion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DailyMotion "DailyMotion"), Samsung, [Vessel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vessel_(website) "Vessel (website)"), and Watchable.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-var-roettgers-15-4) CollegeHumor subsidiary Big Breakfast signed a deal with Verizon's [go90](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Go90 "Go90") streaming service in 2015, which included the show _Fatal Decision_ and a commitment of ten video clips per month for the platform.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-var-roettgers-15-4) During this time, Shane Rahmani served as CollegeHumor's general manager. _Fatal Decision_ was ultimately released on Dropout's own platform in 2025.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-var-roettgers-15-4)

After starting production in 2017, CollegeHumor launched its Dropout TV video platform on September 26, 2018.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Anthony_Ha_TechCrunch-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-fast-company-interview-24-8) CollegeHumor's then-CEO, Rich Cusick, announced the service as a "TV-MA version of CollegeHumor" that would "allow us to double down our investment into premium original content, resulting in a bigger, better, badder CollegeHumor."[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Max_Godnick_Cheddar-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Todd_Spangler_Variety-10) Dropout was also pitched as a way to allow fans to dive deeper into pre-established popular characters and shows from CollegeHumor's YouTube channel.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Max_Godnick_Cheddar-9) CollegeHumor's Chief Creative Officer, [Sam Reich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Reich "Sam Reich"), also claimed that the founding of Dropout was in response to difficulty in receiving advertising dollars on traditional media platforms for mature content.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-11) At launch, Dropout announced a mix of scripted and unscripted content, as well as digital comics and chat-story content and a subscriber-only Discord.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Todd_Spangler_Variety-10)

Dropout utilizes CollegeHumor spinoff [Vimeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vimeo "Vimeo") as its hosting service.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-12) Dropout officially launched native [iOS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IOS "IOS") and [Android](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Android_(operating_system) "Android (operating system)") apps for its service in December 2018, allowing users to watch shows and also cast to smart TVs. Comics and chat stories were also integrated into the app.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-NativeApp-13)

### Independent ownership

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dropout_(streaming_service)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Independent ownership")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/Samreich.jpg/250px-Samreich.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Samreich.jpg)

Dropout CEO [Sam Reich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Reich "Sam Reich") (pictured in 2024) acquired a majority interest in the service in 2020.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-iac-ha-20-14)

After launch, Dropout saw that the unscripted and less expensive content both acquired and retained viewers, while more expensive and scripted shows neither acquired nor retained viewers, with the limited exception of _WTF 101_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Digiday_-_lost_its_early-2)_[Dimension 20](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension\_20 "Dimension 20")_ became the most popular show on the platform, followed by _Um, Actually_ and _Cartoon Hell_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Digiday_-_lost_its_early-2)_[Game Changer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game\_Changer\_(game\_show) "Game Changer (game show)")_, hosted by Reich, would also become a success upon launch in 2019.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Digiday_-_lost_its_early-2) A year after Dropout's launch, the service had between 75,000 and 100,000 subscribers.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Bethy_Squires_Vulture-15) Dropout planned to release a new original title per month in 2019, according to Sam Reich.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Todd_Spangler_Variety-10)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-16) However, the programming slate did not allow Dropout to pivot quickly enough away from scripted content and it was still not profitable by the end of 2019; Reich later noted that "we had a writer's room full of scripted comedy writers. All of us were sort of having to pivot to think about something that wasn't our primary skill set."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-dead-june-12-24-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Peter_Kafka_Recode-18) Because Dropout was in the middle of a $30 million subscription investment, the streamer was on track to "lose" another $10 million by the end of 2019 before it would be profitable.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Peter_Kafka_Recode-18)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Digiday_-_lost_its_early-2)

In January 2020, IAC announced it had ceased financing CollegeHumor, leading to the layoff of 105 employees.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Anthony_Ha_TechCrunch-5)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Bethy_Squires_Vulture-15)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-vulture-like-2009-19) IAC unsuccessfully attempted to sell CollegeHumor to numerous studios and entertainment companies at this time, reportedly seeking up to $100 million for the company;[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-fast-company-interview-24-8)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-20)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Peter_Kafka_Recode-18)[Viacom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount_Global "Paramount Global") offered to buy CollegeHumor and its back catalog for $3 million.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-vulture-like-2009-19) IAC ultimately sold CollegeHumor to Reich, the then-Chief Creative Officer, in 2020, who transitioned to CEO as a result.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-iac-ha-20-14) IAC kept a minority stake in Dropout,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Anthony_Ha_TechCrunch-5) having been convinced by Reich it had the potential to become worth more than Viacom's offer.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-vulture-like-2009-19) The deal was finalized in March 2020.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-fast-company-interview-24-8) Dropout ended production on scripted shows and focused on unscripted shows such as _Um, Actually_, _[Dimension 20](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension\_20 "Dimension 20")_, and _[Game Changer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game\_Changer\_(game\_show) "Game Changer (game show)")_, briefly producing these series through online conference during the beginning of the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

During the July-November [2023 SAG-AFTRA strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_SAG-AFTRA_strike "2023 SAG-AFTRA strike"), Dropout series such as _Dimension 20_, _Game Changer_ and _Um, Actually_ were initially shut down.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Gizmodo_Strike-21) Reich stated:

> Because we aren't associated with the [AMPTP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AMPTP "AMPTP"), it's possible we may be able to reach an interim agreement with [SAG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SAG-AFTRA "SAG-AFTRA") that allows us to continue to produce content during the strike. But we'll only do that, obviously, if we get the blessing of the union and the buy-in of our performers. If not, we have enough content in the can to last us a little past the end of the year.... As for me, I intend to honor my union's position that I not promote SAG productions as a performer – even if they are produced by me. That means that I won't personally be promoting any of our shows for the time being.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-22)

In August 2023, Reich announced that all Dropout shows had resumed production as it was determined that their "New Media Agreement for Non-Dramatic Programming" was actually a non-struck SAG-AFTRA contract.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Dropout_August_2023_Update-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-var-maas-23-25)

Also in August 2023, [NPR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NPR "NPR") stated that "Dropout has not shared their official subscriber count, but Reich says it's in the mid-hundreds of thousands. He's very aware that doesn't come close to the hundreds of millions of subscribers that large media companies have, but, to him, that's not necessarily a problem.... Though they're not required to by unions, he said Dropout is working to become one of the first streamers to pay [residuals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Residual_(entertainment_industry) "Residual (entertainment industry)") to their writers, actors, and crew members".[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-26) Dropout also pays performers to audition.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-fast-company-interview-24-8) Dropout's overall subscriber count almost doubled during 2023;[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-var-maas-23-25) By October 2025, Dropout had over a million subscribers.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-LATimes2025-27)

Dropout officially retired all CollegeHumor branding in September 2023.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-poly-polo-23-28) Later that year, Dropout [shared its profit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Profit_sharing "Profit sharing") with its employees and other workers,[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-esq-sg-24-29)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-var-maas-23-25)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-fast-company-interview-24-8) giving them between a tenth and a fourth of their total earnings.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-vulture-like-2009-19) This practice continued in 2024 for a second year. Additionally, Dropout offers higher-than-average pay to performers: due to its heavy use of prosthetics, actors on _[Very Important People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Very\_Important\_People\_(2023\_TV\_series) "Very Important People (2023 TV series)")_ are paid between $5,000 and $10,000 per episode, and main cast members of _[Dimension 20](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimension\_20 "Dimension 20")_ are paid approximately $7,000 per episode.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-vulture-like-2009-19) Stand-up comedian [Gianmarco Soresi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gianmarco_Soresi "Gianmarco Soresi") made more money filming one episode of _[Game Changer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game\_Changer\_(game\_show) "Game Changer (game show)")_ than he did for his role on the [Paramount+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount+ "Paramount+") show _Crutch_.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-vulture-like-2009-19) Reich himself earned almost nothing during the first two years of Dropout ownership; in 2022 he earned over $1 million.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-vulture-like-2009-19)

Dropout signed an expansion deal with [talent agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talent_agency "Talent agency")[CAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creative_Artists_Agency "Creative Artists Agency") in July 2025.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-dead-grobar-25-30) In August 2025, _[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety\_(magazine) "Variety (magazine)")_ reported that [Brennan Lee Mulligan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brennan_Lee_Mulligan "Brennan Lee Mulligan") had "struck a new three-year development deal at his longtime home media company Dropout".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Variety-2025-31) In the 10th episode of _[Game Changer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game\_Changer\_(game\_show) "Game Changer (game show)")_'s seventh season, [Vic Michaelis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vic_Michaelis "Vic Michaelis") and [Aabria Iyengar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aabria_Iyengar "Aabria Iyengar") were elected as [honorary presidents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honorary_President "Honorary President") of Dropout.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-33)

## Production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dropout_(streaming_service)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Production")]

Dropout is headquartered in [Silver Lake, Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_Lake,_Los_Angeles "Silver Lake, Los Angeles"). The company's production studio includes two sound stages, one for _Dimension 20_ and one which rotates between other productions, as well as an art studio for set and prop design. As of 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dropout_(streaming_service)&action=edit), the company has 40 full-time employees.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-LATimes2025-27)

## Service and availability

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dropout_(streaming_service)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Service and availability")]

Dropout is available worldwide; as of 2024[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dropout_(streaming_service)&action=edit) around 60% of subscribers were in the United States.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-esq-sg-24-29)

### Subscription model

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dropout_(streaming_service)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Subscription model")]

The company has justified the pricing model as allowing them to create content without being dependent on, or beholden to, requests from advertisers.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-34) In December 2018, visitors to the service spent on average 31 minutes per visit, and visited on average 3.5 times per week.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-NativeApp-13) Throughout 2019, Dropout began to experiment with more live streaming versions of their shows, through using [Twitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitch_(service) "Twitch (service)") and podcast-like formats. At the end of 2023, the average user subscribed for 18 months; Reich said in June 2024 that the statistic is continuing to increase.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-var-maas-23-25)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-fast-company-interview-24-8)As of June 2024[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dropout_(streaming_service)&action=edit), Dropout earns around 80–85% of its revenue via subscriptions.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-fast-company-interview-24-8)

Dropout launched with a beta price of $3.99 per month for the first three months of the service. After December 2018, the price rose to a three tiered option, with monthly memberships for $5.99/month, semi-annual memberships for $4.99/month, and annual memberships for $3.99/month.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-35)As of January 2022[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dropout_(streaming_service)&action=edit), new subscribers paid $5.99 monthly or $59.99 yearly, while those who already subscribed prior to that date were charged $4.99 monthly or $47.99 yearly.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Dec_2021_tweet-36) In April 2025, Dropout announced a subscription cost increase ($6.99 monthly or $69.99 annually) which took effect on May 7, 2025. However, this increase did not impact existing subscribers who were [grandfathered in](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandfathered_in "Grandfathered in") to the legacy subscription cost.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-38)

In August 2019, CollegeHumor partnered with [Facebook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facebook "Facebook") to offer Dropout content via paid video subscriptions on Facebook's platform.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-39) Users are also able to access Dropout content through YouTube via the join function.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In October 2025, CEO Sam Reich announced a "Superfan" subscription for $129.99 a year, described as a 'Pay more if you feel like it' tier. Perks include behind the scenes content, discounts and additional items in Dropout's online store, and early access to purchase tickets for live events.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-40)

### Services

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dropout_(streaming_service)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Services")]

In addition to original series, Dropout offered videos produced by CollegeHumor 72 hours before they were released to the public. Previously, a subscriber-only [Discord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discord_(software) "Discord (software)") server was included as a service, later expanded to non-subscribers as well, until its closure on May 26, 2024. Dropout also has a store which sells merchandise (such as shirts, stickers, and mugs) related to shows on the platform.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-41)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-42)

In February 2026, Dropout announced that British surrealist [adult puppet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adult_puppeteering "Adult puppeteering") musical [comedy horror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_horror "Comedy horror") web series _[Don't Hug Me I'm Scared](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don't\_Hug\_Me\_I'm\_Scared "Don't Hug Me I'm Scared")_ would be non-exclusively licensed to them for three years, in the first-ever licensing deal for Dropout.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-43)

## Original shows

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dropout_(streaming_service)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Original shows")]

See also: [CollegeHumor §List of CH Originals series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CollegeHumor#List_of_CH_Originals_series "CollegeHumor")

Shows on Dropout are usually released [fortnightly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortnight "Fortnight"), a schedule used more often for podcasts than for television.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-var-maas-23-25) Dropout planned to release a new original title per month in 2019, according to Sam Reich.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-Todd_Spangler_Variety-10)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-54) By 2020, the service had retired all scripted shows in favor of cheaper and more successful unscripted content.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-poly-polo-23-28)

_Dirty Laundry_, _Play It By Ear_, and _[Make Some Noise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Make\_Some\_Noise\_(TV\_series) "Make Some Noise (TV series)")_, each spun off from _Game Changer_, premiered throughout 2022. In 2023, Dropout started airing the improvisational interview show _[Very Important People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Very\_Important\_People\_(2023\_TV\_series) "Very Important People (2023 TV series)")_, and in 2024 six new shows premiered: _Smartypants_, _Thousandaires_, _Dropout Presents_, _Monét's Slumber Party_, _Gastronauts_, and _Nobody Asked_.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-npr-luse-24-55)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-ta-champagne-24-56)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-brown-int-yt-24-57)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-var-maas-monet-24-49)

A show called _Parlor Room_, hosted by Becca Scott, was announced in March 2025 and premiered on April 18, 2025.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-pr-sheehan-25-58) A fourth _Game Changer_ spinoff, _Crowd Control_, premiered on September 8, 2025.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-vulture-like-2009-19)

As of October 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Dropout_(streaming_service)&action=edit), an untitled animated show was in development.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-LATimes2025-27) A livestream channel titled _Dropout 24/7_, which airs Dropout shows continuously, launched on February 18, 2026; this channel is exclusive to the Dropout platform. The channel began with a [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_(media) "Marathon (media)") of _Dimension 20_.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-59)

Dropout Improv is an [improvisational comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Improvisational_comedy "Improvisational comedy") tour featuring regular Dropout performers, it has toured both North America and the United Kingdom.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-var-maas-di-25-115)

A panel event called "Cue the Chaos: In Convo with Dropout Improv" took place at the [Just for Laughs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just_for_Laughs "Just for Laughs") comedy festival in [Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal "Montreal") on July 26, 2025.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-jpr-25-116) Sam Reich also appeared at a "fireside chat" on July 24 as one of the festival's more exclusive "ComedyPRO" events.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-reich-jfl-25-117)

Dates for a Dropout Improv tour in [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia") and [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand "New Zealand") are scheduled in 2026 for [Perth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perth "Perth"), [Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney "Sydney"), [Melbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne "Melbourne"), and [Auckland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland "Auckland").[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dropout_(streaming_service)#cite_note-aur-santos-25-118)

He was born on September 14, 1942 in Newton Center, Massachusetts, one of six Boston-Irish children born to Patrick and Alice Joyce Lydon. In 1961, he graduated from the Roxbury Latin School, the oldest US school in continuous existence, and entered Yale University. In his _Yale Daily News_ column, _In A Mellow Tone_, Michael wrote one of the first published articles on the Beatles, who were then unknown in the US. In the summer of 1964 working as stringer for the _Boston Globe_, he went to Mississippi to cover the civil rights struggle including the violent KKK murders of three civil rights activists. On graduation from Yale, Michael joined _Newsweek_ in “Swinging London,” interviewing the Beatles’ John Lennon and Paul McCartney. Newsweek transferred Michael to San Francisco just in time for the Human Be-in, the prelude to the Summer of Love, and the emergence of hippie rock. In 1967, he became the founding editor of _Rolling Stone_ magazine. Following this, working as a freelance journalist, he went on the road with musical heavyweights BB King, Johnny Cash, the Grateful Dead. He was part of a long tour with the Rolling Stones ending in the wild Altamont Free Concert. These dramatic experiences became the basis for his first book, _Rock Folk_. ![Image 2](https://yale1965.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/lydon-bw.jpg)After his years of listening and writing about music, Michael learned to play the guitar, the harmonica and to whistle at the competitive level. He met and started performing with his future wife, Ellen Mandel. They climbed every stage they could find, including a San Francisco talent show with Robin Williams. Still, he found time to write his second book, _Boogie Lighting, How music became electric_. In the early seventies, Michael and Ellen moved from California to New York’s East Village, joining many young hopefuls trying to get ahead in the music business. They played when and wherever there was an audience – Michael in the subway, and as a duo in colleges and rock clubs. They opened for Muddy Waters, Manhattan Transfer, Mose Allison among others. In the ’90s, Michael researched and wrote the definitive biography, _Ray Charles, Man and Music_. ![Image 3](https://yale1965.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/lydon-red.jpg)Michael’s books span an enormous range: _Writing & Life_ (the Bible to Nabokov), _Real Writing_ (Balzac, Dreier et al), _How to Play Classic Guitar_, _How to Write Songs for Fun (and maybe) Profit_. Among his many songs are _And So It Goes, Love at First Sight, Paris in the Rain, Do You Remember_. Michael lived for over fifty years with the love of his life, Ellen Mandel, lieder, stage composer and singer. In addition to Ellen, he leaves behind his daughter Shuna and her partner Charles, and his brothers Peter of Berkeley and Christopher of Boston. Michael Lydon was an accomplished performer, writer, composer and music critic. He was a lifelong seeker and loving person who will be greatly missed by his many friends and extended family members. _“Songs, I like to think, are the unfinished symphonies of daily life, works of art, both lovable and profound, that we hum as we walk here and there on soon-forgotten errands”_ — Michael Lydon P.S. An appreciation of Michael by T.S. Phillips at the site, One Man’s Guitar (including a wonderful performance by Michael of “What a Lovesick Fool was I”). [Click here.](https://onemanz.com/guitar/michael-lydon-1942-2025-an-appreciation/) * * * **OBITUARY** ## Michael Lydon, Writer Who Rocked With the 1960s, Dies at 82 **A founding editor of Rolling Stone and a seasoned music journalist, he spent time with the Beatles and toured with the Grateful Dead and the Rolling Stones.** By Alex Williams, _New York Times_ ![Image 4](https://yale1965.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/mlydon01.jpg) The music journalist Michael Lydon in 1967. He met Jann Wenner at the Monterey International Pop Festival that year and was offered a job at Mr. Wenner’s new magazine, Rolling Stone. Credit: The Baron Alan Wolman Collection, Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Michael Lydon, who recovered from a galling pan of the Beatles for his college newspaper to become a founding editor of _Rolling Stone_ and a pioneering rock journalist, capturing the pinwheel vibrancy of Swinging London and flower-power San Francisco, died on July 30 in Manhattan. He was 82. His wife, Ellen Mandel, said he died in a hospital of complications from Parkinson’s disease. Writing for publications such as _Newsweek_, _The Boston Globe_ and _The New York Times_ as well as _Rolling Stone_, Mr. Lydon mingled with the towering figures of the rapidly evolving rock era: Jimi Hendrix, Janis Joplin, the Grateful Dead and the Rolling Stones. As a young _Newsweek_ correspondent fresh from Yale University, Mr. Lydon arrived in London in the mid-1960s — a time when the postwar generation, with its taste for avant-garde fashion and rafter-rattling rock, was aiming to blast the bowler hats from the heads of the country’s traditionalists. It was there that he met the Beatles, whom he had derided as “poor foreign imitations” of the American rock ‘n’ roll originals in a 1964 article for _The Yale Daily News_. “Whenever the first strains of ‘I Want to Hold Your Hand’ begin to twitch my stirrup bones,” he wrote, “I send out silent screams for help to Chuck Berry, Elvis” and others “who have long defended the American way of rock.” His view changed after the Beatles’ landmark 1965 album, “Rubber Soul,” with its nuanced and introspective songwriting and Dylanesque shadings. The album seemed to change the Beatles’ view of themselves, too. “You don’t know us now if you don’t know ‘Rubber Soul,’” John Lennon told Mr. Lydon in a 1966 interview. “All our ideas are different now.” ![Image 5](https://yale1965.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/mlydon02.jpg) Mr. Lydon in 2015. Writing for Rolling Stone and other publications in the 1960s, he mingled with towering figures like Jimi Hendrix, Janis Joplin, the Grateful Dead and the Rolling Stones. Credit: Ellen Mandel _Newsweek_ transferred Mr. Lydon to San Francisco in 1967, when the Haight-Ashbury hippie scene was in full flower. “The Fillmore and Avalon Ballrooms were my beat,” he recalled on his website, “Janis Joplin and Jerry Garcia my inside sources.” He bore witness to rock history that same year when he covered the Monterey International Pop Festival, now remembered as the apotheosis of the psychedelic era. From the press section, Mr. Lydon took in Hendrix, the Who and dozens of other luminaries and “let my mind be blown,” he recalled. “Exciting days — kids my own age beaming big ideas through electric music. At concerts and communes I heard friendly encouragement to be myself. I let my hair grow long and quit _Newsweek_.” He also met Jann Wenner, who was starting a new magazine for and by the rock generation, to be called _Rolling Stone_, and soon offered Mr. Lydon a job as one of his top lieutenants. “You could look at the guy” and see “gears moving in his head,” Mr. Lydon was quoted as saying of his onetime boss in Joe Hagan’s “Sticky Fingers: The Life and Times of Jann Wenner and _Rolling Stone Magazine_” (2017). For the magazine’s first issue, dated Nov. 9, 1967, Mr. Lydon wrote an investigative article on the wobbly financial underpinnings of Monterey Pop, which had yet to direct much of its proceeds to philanthropic causes, a stated goal. “In ironic fact,” he wrote, “what happened at the Festival and its financial affairs looks like the traditional Charity Ball in hippie drag.” ![Image 6](https://yale1965.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/mlydon03.jpg) Mr. Lydon in the early 1970s, around the time he turned to writing and performing music in addition to writing about it. Credit: Ellen Mandel Succumbing to the turn on/tune in/drop out spirit of the times, Mr. Lydon left his post at _Rolling Stone_ after a few issues and moved to a hippie hut near Mendocino, the storied bohemian coastal hamlet north of San Francisco. He nonetheless continued to write for _Rolling Stone_, including a 1969 Grateful Dead tour chronicle in which he noted the bummer vibes spreading through the counterculture: “What San Francisco started has become so diffuse, copied, extended, exploited, rebelled against, and simply accepted that it has become nearly invisible.” That article, dated Aug. 23, 1969, was published just weeks after the Manson “family” murders in Los Angeles — an event often cited as the end of the ’60s dream. Later that year, Mr. Lydon wrangled an invitation to travel with the Rolling Stones during its seismic American tour, which culminated with the violence-marred Altamont Speedway Free Festival near San Francisco, another terminal blow to the peace-and-love ideal. “The only common emotion is disappointment and impotent sorrow,” Mr. Lydon wrote of the Altamont festival’s legacy in his 1971 book, “Rock Folk: Portraits From the Rock ‘n’ Roll Pantheon.” “‘If only… if only…” ![Image 7](https://yale1965.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/mlydon04.jpg) “The only common emotion,” Mr. Lydon wrote in the wake of the disastrous Altamont festival in “Rock Folk” (1971), “is disappointment and impotent sorrow.” Credit: Citadel Michael Clery Lydon was born on Sept. 14, 1942, in Boston, the fifth of six children of Patrick and Alice (Joyce) Lydon. His father was a foreman at the local telephone company. He earned a scholarship to the prestigious Roxbury Latin School and, after graduating in 1961, won another to attend Yale, where he received a bachelor’s degree in American history in 1965. Early in his career, Mr. Lydon covered hard news, including the aftermath of the grisly 1964 murders of three young voter registration activists in Mississippi, a signature event in the civil rights movement. Swept up in the times, he turned his attention to writing about music — and, by the dawn of the 1970s, to writing and performing music himself, learning the trade with a flat-top Gibson guitar and a Bob Dylan songbook. “As soon as I could play the two chords of Bo Diddley’s ‘I’m a Man,’ I was launched,” he recalled. ![Image 8](https://yale1965.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/mlydon05.jpg) In the early 1970s, Mr. Lydon formed a cabaret act with Ellen Mandel, whom he began dating in 1970 and married in 1981. Credit: via Ellen Mandel With his eclectic musical tastes, he formed a cabaret act with Ms. Mandel, who played piano and sang, and whom he began dating in 1970 and married in 1981. Starting in the late 1990s, Mr. Lydon released four albums of pop-jazz on Brite Records, a label he started with his wife. He also developed a nightclub comedy act called “The Handsomest Man in the World.” He never abandoned writing; he published nearly 20 books over the years, including “Ray Charles: Man and Music” (1998) and “The Rolling Stones Discover America” (1970), his account of the band’s star-crossed 1969 tour. ![Image 9](https://yale1965.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/mlydon06.jpg) Among Mr. Lydon’s many books was a biography of Ray Charles, published in 1998. Credit: Riverhead Books In addition to his wife, Mr. Lydon is survived by his daughter, Shuna Lydon, from his first marriage, to Susan Gordon — a writer who worked with him at _Rolling Stone_ and, as Susan Lydon, became a noted feminist author — which ended in divorce; and two brothers, Peter and Christopher. In a 2015 interview with _The Wooster Blade_, a high school newspaper in Ohio, Mr. Lydon recalled how the music he covered during the 1960s led to his own evolving creative sensibility. “Bob Dylan put out a song that said, ‘He not busy being born is busy dying,’ and I was trying to apply it to myself,” he said. “So it was not just the sound in the music, but the ideas in the music that I found really, really interesting and challenging.” Alex Williams is a _Times_ reporter on the Obituaries desk.

He was born on September 14, 1942 in Newton Center, Massachusetts, one of six Boston-Irish children born to Patrick and Alice Joyce Lydon. In 1961, he graduated from the Roxbury Latin School, the oldest US school in continuous existence, and entered Yale University. In his _Yale Daily News_ column, _In A Mellow Tone_, Michael wrote one of the first published articles on the Beatles, who were then unknown in the US. In the summer of 1964 working as stringer for the _Boston Globe_, he went to Mississippi to cover the civil rights struggle including the violent KKK murders of three civil rights activists. On graduation from Yale, Michael joined _Newsweek_ in “Swinging London,” interviewing the Beatles’ John Lennon and Paul McCartney. Newsweek transferred Michael to San Francisco just in time for the Human Be-in, the prelude to the Summer of Love, and the emergence of hippie rock. In 1967, he became the founding editor of _Rolling Stone_ magazine. Following this, working as a freelance journalist, he went on the road with musical heavyweights BB King, Johnny Cash, the Grateful Dead. He was part of a long tour with the Rolling Stones ending in the wild Altamont Free Concert. These dramatic experiences became the basis for his first book, _Rock Folk_. ![Image 2](https://yale1965.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/lydon-bw.jpg)After his years of listening and writing about music, Michael learned to play the guitar, the harmonica and to whistle at the competitive level. He met and started performing with his future wife, Ellen Mandel. They climbed every stage they could find, including a San Francisco talent show with Robin Williams. Still, he found time to write his second book, _Boogie Lighting, How music became electric_. In the early seventies, Michael and Ellen moved from California to New York’s East Village, joining many young hopefuls trying to get ahead in the music business. They played when and wherever there was an audience – Michael in the subway, and as a duo in colleges and rock clubs. They opened for Muddy Waters, Manhattan Transfer, Mose Allison among others. In the ’90s, Michael researched and wrote the definitive biography, _Ray Charles, Man and Music_. ![Image 3](https://yale1965.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/lydon-red.jpg)Michael’s books span an enormous range: _Writing & Life_ (the Bible to Nabokov), _Real Writing_ (Balzac, Dreier et al), _How to Play Classic Guitar_, _How to Write Songs for Fun (and maybe) Profit_. Among his many songs are _And So It Goes, Love at First Sight, Paris in the Rain, Do You Remember_. Michael lived for over fifty years with the love of his life, Ellen Mandel, lieder, stage composer and singer. In addition to Ellen, he leaves behind his daughter Shuna and her partner Charles, and his brothers Peter of Berkeley and Christopher of Boston. Michael Lydon was an accomplished performer, writer, composer and music critic. He was a lifelong seeker and loving person who will be greatly missed by his many friends and extended family members. _“Songs, I like to think, are the unfinished symphonies of daily life, works of art, both lovable and profound, that we hum as we walk here and there on soon-forgotten errands”_ — Michael Lydon P.S. An appreciation of Michael by T.S. Phillips at the site, One Man’s Guitar (including a wonderful performance by Michael of “What a Lovesick Fool was I”). [Click here.](https://onemanz.com/guitar/michael-lydon-1942-2025-an-appreciation/) * * * **OBITUARY** ## Michael Lydon, Writer Who Rocked With the 1960s, Dies at 82 **A founding editor of Rolling Stone and a seasoned music journalist, he spent time with the Beatles and toured with the Grateful Dead and the Rolling Stones.** By Alex Williams, _New York Times_ ![Image 4](https://yale1965.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/mlydon01.jpg) The music journalist Michael Lydon in 1967. He met Jann Wenner at the Monterey International Pop Festival that year and was offered a job at Mr. Wenner’s new magazine, Rolling Stone. Credit: The Baron Alan Wolman Collection, Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Michael Lydon, who recovered from a galling pan of the Beatles for his college newspaper to become a founding editor of _Rolling Stone_ and a pioneering rock journalist, capturing the pinwheel vibrancy of Swinging London and flower-power San Francisco, died on July 30 in Manhattan. He was 82. His wife, Ellen Mandel, said he died in a hospital of complications from Parkinson’s disease. Writing for publications such as _Newsweek_, _The Boston Globe_ and _The New York Times_ as well as _Rolling Stone_, Mr. Lydon mingled with the towering figures of the rapidly evolving rock era: Jimi Hendrix, Janis Joplin, the Grateful Dead and the Rolling Stones. As a young _Newsweek_ correspondent fresh from Yale University, Mr. Lydon arrived in London in the mid-1960s — a time when the postwar generation, with its taste for avant-garde fashion and rafter-rattling rock, was aiming to blast the bowler hats from the heads of the country’s traditionalists. It was there that he met the Beatles, whom he had derided as “poor foreign imitations” of the American rock ‘n’ roll originals in a 1964 article for _The Yale Daily News_. “Whenever the first strains of ‘I Want to Hold Your Hand’ begin to twitch my stirrup bones,” he wrote, “I send out silent screams for help to Chuck Berry, Elvis” and others “who have long defended the American way of rock.” His view changed after the Beatles’ landmark 1965 album, “Rubber Soul,” with its nuanced and introspective songwriting and Dylanesque shadings. The album seemed to change the Beatles’ view of themselves, too. “You don’t know us now if you don’t know ‘Rubber Soul,’” John Lennon told Mr. Lydon in a 1966 interview. “All our ideas are different now.” ![Image 5](https://yale1965.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/mlydon02.jpg) Mr. Lydon in 2015. Writing for Rolling Stone and other publications in the 1960s, he mingled with towering figures like Jimi Hendrix, Janis Joplin, the Grateful Dead and the Rolling Stones. Credit: Ellen Mandel _Newsweek_ transferred Mr. Lydon to San Francisco in 1967, when the Haight-Ashbury hippie scene was in full flower. “The Fillmore and Avalon Ballrooms were my beat,” he recalled on his website, “Janis Joplin and Jerry Garcia my inside sources.” He bore witness to rock history that same year when he covered the Monterey International Pop Festival, now remembered as the apotheosis of the psychedelic era. From the press section, Mr. Lydon took in Hendrix, the Who and dozens of other luminaries and “let my mind be blown,” he recalled. “Exciting days — kids my own age beaming big ideas through electric music. At concerts and communes I heard friendly encouragement to be myself. I let my hair grow long and quit _Newsweek_.” He also met Jann Wenner, who was starting a new magazine for and by the rock generation, to be called _Rolling Stone_, and soon offered Mr. Lydon a job as one of his top lieutenants. “You could look at the guy” and see “gears moving in his head,” Mr. Lydon was quoted as saying of his onetime boss in Joe Hagan’s “Sticky Fingers: The Life and Times of Jann Wenner and _Rolling Stone Magazine_” (2017). For the magazine’s first issue, dated Nov. 9, 1967, Mr. Lydon wrote an investigative article on the wobbly financial underpinnings of Monterey Pop, which had yet to direct much of its proceeds to philanthropic causes, a stated goal. “In ironic fact,” he wrote, “what happened at the Festival and its financial affairs looks like the traditional Charity Ball in hippie drag.” ![Image 6](https://yale1965.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/mlydon03.jpg) Mr. Lydon in the early 1970s, around the time he turned to writing and performing music in addition to writing about it. Credit: Ellen Mandel Succumbing to the turn on/tune in/drop out spirit of the times, Mr. Lydon left his post at _Rolling Stone_ after a few issues and moved to a hippie hut near Mendocino, the storied bohemian coastal hamlet north of San Francisco. He nonetheless continued to write for _Rolling Stone_, including a 1969 Grateful Dead tour chronicle in which he noted the bummer vibes spreading through the counterculture: “What San Francisco started has become so diffuse, copied, extended, exploited, rebelled against, and simply accepted that it has become nearly invisible.” That article, dated Aug. 23, 1969, was published just weeks after the Manson “family” murders in Los Angeles — an event often cited as the end of the ’60s dream. Later that year, Mr. Lydon wrangled an invitation to travel with the Rolling Stones during its seismic American tour, which culminated with the violence-marred Altamont Speedway Free Festival near San Francisco, another terminal blow to the peace-and-love ideal. “The only common emotion is disappointment and impotent sorrow,” Mr. Lydon wrote of the Altamont festival’s legacy in his 1971 book, “Rock Folk: Portraits From the Rock ‘n’ Roll Pantheon.” “‘If only… if only…” ![Image 7](https://yale1965.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/mlydon04.jpg) “The only common emotion,” Mr. Lydon wrote in the wake of the disastrous Altamont festival in “Rock Folk” (1971), “is disappointment and impotent sorrow.” Credit: Citadel Michael Clery Lydon was born on Sept. 14, 1942, in Boston, the fifth of six children of Patrick and Alice (Joyce) Lydon. # Mike Lydon

![Image 5: mike lydon](https://seasideinstitute.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/MPL-headshot216.webp)

## Mike Lydon

Fellow  
2017 Seaside Prize Winner

* * *

Mike Lydon is a Principal with Street Plans and leads the firm’s New York City office. Mike is an internationally recognized planner, writer, speaker, and advocate for livable cities. NPR, The New York Times, CNN Headline News, ABC News, City Lab, Planetizen, Salon, Next City, Architect Magazine, and Streetsblog have featured his work, among other publications.

Mike is the creator of The Open Streets Project and the globally acclaimed Tactical Urbanism: Short-Term Action, Long-Term Change Vol.1 – 4.With Tony Garcia, Mike is the recipient of the 2017 Seaside Prize and co-author of Tactical Urbanism (Island Press, 2015), named by Planetizen as one of the top ten planning books of the year. Mike collaborated with Andres Duany and Jeff Speck in writing The Smart Growth Manual (McGraw-Hill, 2009).

A founding member of the New England Chapter of the Congress for the New Urbanism, a Board Member for CNU New York, and a steering committee member of the Next Generation of New Urbanists, he remains active in both local and national planning, design, and smart growth advocacy issues. He lectures frequently and leads workshops and trainings on the topics of smart growth, tactical urbanism, and complete streets/active transportation. Before launching the firm in 2009, Mike worked for Smart Growth Vermont, the Massachusetts Bicycle Coalition, and Ann Arbor’s Get Downtown Program. From 2006 – 2009 Lydon worked for Duany Plater-Zyberk and Company (DPZ), an international leader in the practice of smart growth planning, design, and research techniques.

Mike currently serves on Transportation Alternative’s Executive Committee for the New York City Harbor Ring project, and is an advisor to the Bicycle Coalition of Maine. Mike received a B.A. in American Cultural Studies from Bates College and a Masters in Urban Planning from the University of Michigan. He encourages you to trade four wheels for two.

# Mike Lydon

![Image 5: mike lydon](https://seasideinstitute.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/MPL-headshot216.webp)

## Mike Lydon

Fellow  
2017 Seaside Prize Winner

* * *

Mike Lydon is a Principal with Street Plans and leads the firm’s New York City office. Mike is an internationally recognized planner, writer, speaker, and advocate for livable cities. NPR, The New York Times, CNN Headline News, ABC News, City Lab, Planetizen, Salon, Next City, Architect Magazine, and Streetsblog have featured his work, among other publications.

Mike is the creator of The Open Streets Project and the globally acclaimed Tactical Urbanism: Short-Term Action, Long-Term Change Vol.1 – 4.With Tony Garcia, Mike is the recipient of the 2017 Seaside Prize and co-author of Tactical Urbanism (Island Press, 2015), named by Planetizen as one of the top ten planning books of the year. Mike collaborated with Andres Duany and Jeff Speck in writing The Smart Growth Manual (McGraw-Hill, 2009).

A founding member of the New England Chapter of the Congress for the New Urbanism, a Board Member for CNU New York, and a steering committee member of the Next Generation of New Urbanists, he remains active in both local and national planning, design, and smart growth advocacy issues. He lectures frequently and leads workshops and trainings on the topics of smart growth, tactical urbanism, and complete streets/active transportation. Before launching the firm in 2009, Mike worked for Smart Growth Vermont, the Massachusetts Bicycle Coalition, and Ann Arbor’s Get Downtown Program. From 2006 – 2009 Lydon worked for Duany Plater-Zyberk and Company (DPZ), an international leader in the practice of smart growth planning, design, and research techniques.

Mike currently serves on Transportation Alternative’s Executive Committee for the New York City Harbor Ring project, and is an advisor to the Bicycle Coalition of Maine. Mike received a B.A. in American Cultural Studies from Bates College and a Masters in Urban Planning from the University of Michigan. He encourages you to trade four wheels for two.

# Mike Lydon

Principal

Street Plans

Brooklyn, New York 

[Website](http://www.street-plans.com/)

* * *

[Bio](https://www.usgbc.org/people/mike-lydon/0011261107?view=overview)[Courses](https://www.usgbc.org/people/mike-lydon/0011261107?view=courses)[Articles](https://www.usgbc.org/people/mike-lydon/0011261107?view=articles)

Mike Lydon is a Principal with Street Plans and leads the firm’s New York City office. Mike is an internationally recognized planner, writer, speaker, and advocate for livable cities. His work has been featured in NPR, The New York Times, CNN Headline News, Monocle, ABC News, City Lab, Planetizen, Salon, Next City, Architect Magazine, and Streetsblog among other publications.

Mike is the creator of the The Open Streets Project and the globally acclaimed Tactical Urbanism: Short-Term Action, Long-Term Change Vol. 1 – 5. With Tony Garcia, Mike is the recipient of the 2017 Seaside Prize and co-author of Tactical Urbanism (Island Press, 2015), named by Planetizen as one of the top ten planning books of the year. Mike collaborated with Andres Duany and Jeff Speck in writing The Smart Growth Manual (McGraw-Hill, 2009).

A founding member of the New England Chapter of the Congress for the New Urbanism, a Board Member for CNU New York, and a steering committee member of the Next Generation of New Urbanists, he remains active in both local and national planning, design, and smart growth advocacy issues. He lectures frequently and leads workshops and trainings on the topics of smart growth, tactical urbanism, and complete streets/active transportation. Before launching the firm in 2009, Mike worked for Smart Growth Vermont, the Massachusetts Bicycle Coalition, and Ann Arbor’s GetDowntown Program. From 2006 – 2009 Lydon worked for Duany Plater-Zyberk and Company (DPZ), an international leader in the practice of smart growth planning, design, and research techniques.

Mike currently serves on Transportation Alternative’s Executive Committee for the New York City Harbor Ring project, and is an advisor to the Bicycle Coalition of Maine. Mike received a B.A. in American Cultural Studies from Bates College and a Masters in Urban Planning from the University of Michigan. He encourages you to trade four wheels for two.

# Mike Lydon

Principal

Street Plans

Brooklyn, New York 

[Website](http://www.street-plans.com/)

* * *

[Bio](https://www.usgbc.org/people/mike-lydon/0011261107?view=overview)[Courses](https://www.usgbc.org/people/mike-lydon/0011261107?view=courses)[Articles](https://www.usgbc.org/people/mike-lydon/0011261107?view=articles)

Mike Lydon is a Principal with Street Plans and leads the firm’s New York City office. Mike is an internationally recognized planner, writer, speaker, and advocate for livable cities. His work has been featured in NPR, The New York Times, CNN Headline News, Monocle, ABC News, City Lab, Planetizen, Salon, Next City, Architect Magazine, and Streetsblog among other publications.

Mike is the creator of the The Open Streets Project and the globally acclaimed Tactical Urbanism: Short-Term Action, Long-Term Change Vol. 1 – 5. With Tony Garcia, Mike is the recipient of the 2017 Seaside Prize and co-author of Tactical Urbanism (Island Press, 2015), named by Planetizen as one of the top ten planning books of the year. Mike collaborated with Andres Duany and Jeff Speck in writing The Smart Growth Manual (McGraw-Hill, 2009).

A founding member of the New England Chapter of the Congress for the New Urbanism, a Board Member for CNU New York, and a steering committee member of the Next Generation of New Urbanists, he remains active in both local and national planning, design, and smart growth advocacy issues. He lectures frequently and leads workshops and trainings on the topics of smart growth, tactical urbanism, and complete streets/active transportation. Before launching the firm in 2009, Mike worked for Smart Growth Vermont, the Massachusetts Bicycle Coalition, and Ann Arbor’s GetDowntown Program. From 2006 – 2009 Lydon worked for Duany Plater-Zyberk and Company (DPZ), an international leader in the practice of smart growth planning, design, and research techniques.

Mike currently serves on Transportation Alternative’s Executive Committee for the New York City Harbor Ring project, and is an advisor to the Bicycle Coalition of Maine. Mike received a B.A. in American Cultural Studies from Bates College and a Masters in Urban Planning from the University of Michigan. He encourages you to trade four wheels for two.

# Michael Lydon

![Image 14](https://www.rocksbackpages.com/public/img/writers/821.jpg?updatedAt=2025-08-09-13-35-57)

A _Rolling Stone_ legend of the late '60s and '70s, Michael's seminal pieces on the Rolling Stones et al. were collected in _Rock Folk_ and _Boogie Lightning. Ray Charles: Man and Music_, his biography of the Genius, received glowing reviews. He was also a guitarist-singer-songwriter who performed in New York and released albums such as _Love at First Sight_ (Brite Records). Michael died in New York City on 30th July, 2025.

This is what he wrote when he joined Rock's Backpages:

"I've loved music ever since I wore out Billie Holiday and Duke Ellington records in high school. 'Hit the Road Jack' introduced me to Ray Charles. A girlfriend turned me on to Chuck Berry, and we dug James Brown at the Apollo. In '64 I panned the Beatles in the college paper and praised Martha and the Vandellas instead — my first rock writing. After covering civil rights in Mississippi, I reported on "Swinging London" for _Newsweek_. An interview with John — abrasive — and Paul — charming — converted me to the Beatles. Then I transferred to San Francisco as Haight-Ashbury hippies made headliness. The Fillmore was my beat; Janis and Jerry my inside sources. At Montery Pop I sat mindblown in the press section.

"Exciting days. My hair grew, I quit _Newsweek_, helped start _Rolling Stone_, hitch-hiked to LA to join the Rolling Stones on the wild ride to Altamont. My first book, _Rock Folk_, reflects the tumult of the times, writing now collected in _FLASHBACKS_ (Routledge US/GB).

"In the 70s I met pianist Ellen Mandel and got a Gibson flat-top, a harmonica, a Bob Dylan songbook, and started writing songs and climbing on stages. We worked unpaid with the equally unknown Robin Williams. I wrote my second book, _Boogie Lightning_. We moved to New York, opened for Muddy Waters in Boston. In the '90s I wrote _Ray Charles: Man and Music_. Today I'm writing books and playing East Village clubs with a jazz combo. When I get back grins from couples singing the chorus, I thank the greats who inspired me, but I'm also thinking, 'Look out world, here comes Michael Lydon!'"

**Books**:

_Rock Folk_ (1971)   
_Boogie Lightning_ (1975)   
_How to Succeed in Show Business by Really Trying_ (1985)   
_Writing and Life_ (1995)   
_Ray Charles: Man and Music_ (1999)   
_Flashbacks_ (2003)

**CDs**:

_Love at First Sight_ (1999) (Brite Records)   
_Mike on Mike_ (2002) (Brite Records)

# Michael Lydon

![Image 14](https://www.rocksbackpages.com/public/img/writers/821.jpg?updatedAt=2025-08-09-13-35-57)

A _Rolling Stone_ legend of the late '60s and '70s, Michael's seminal pieces on the Rolling Stones et al. were collected in _Rock Folk_ and _Boogie Lightning. Ray Charles: Man and Music_, his biography of the Genius, received glowing reviews. He was also a guitarist-singer-songwriter who performed in New York and released albums such as _Love at First Sight_ (Brite Records). Michael died in New York City on 30th July, 2025.

This is what he wrote when he joined Rock's Backpages:

"I've loved music ever since I wore out Billie Holiday and Duke Ellington records in high school. 'Hit the Road Jack' introduced me to Ray Charles. A girlfriend turned me on to Chuck Berry, and we dug James Brown at the Apollo. In '64 I panned the Beatles in the college paper and praised Martha and the Vandellas instead — my first rock writing. After covering civil rights in Mississippi, I reported on "Swinging London" for _Newsweek_. An interview with John — abrasive — and Paul — charming — converted me to the Beatles. Then I transferred to San Francisco as Haight-Ashbury hippies made headliness. The Fillmore was my beat; Janis and Jerry my inside sources. At Montery Pop I sat mindblown in the press section.

"Exciting days. My hair grew, I quit _Newsweek_, helped start _Rolling Stone_, hitch-hiked to LA to join the Rolling Stones on the wild ride to Altamont. My first book, _Rock Folk_, reflects the tumult of the times, writing now collected in _FLASHBACKS_ (Routledge US/GB).

"In the 70s I met pianist Ellen Mandel and got a Gibson flat-top, a harmonica, a Bob Dylan songbook, and started writing songs and climbing on stages. We worked unpaid with the equally unknown Robin Williams. I wrote my second book, _Boogie Lightning_. We moved to New York, opened for Muddy Waters in Boston. In the '90s I wrote _Ray Charles: Man and Music_. Today I'm writing books and playing East Village clubs with a jazz combo. When I get back grins from couples singing the chorus, I thank the greats who inspired me, but I'm also thinking, 'Look out world, here comes Michael Lydon!'"

**Books**:

_Rock Folk_ (1971)   
_Boogie Lightning_ (1975)   
_How to Succeed in Show Business by Really Trying_ (1985)   
_Writing and Life_ (1995)   
_Ray Charles: Man and Music_ (1999)   
_Flashbacks_ (2003)

**CDs**:

_Love at First Sight_ (1999) (Brite Records)   
_Mike on Mike_ (2002) (Brite Records)

Michael Lydon had a storied career as a music journalist. He interviewed the Beatles, toured with the Rollings Stones and B.B. King, covered the Monterey International Pop Festival and Altamont, was a founding editor of _Rolling Stone_, considered Jerry Garcia and Janis Joplin his Haight-Ashbury inside sources, and wrote several books on music and writing. He was also a contributor to this journal and member of our editorial board. Michael passed away during the summer of 2025.

As a student at Yale in 1964, Michael said that he “begged everybody to listen to my jazz records, but all anyone wanted to hear was the stupid blue-black LP with the four jerks staring blankly out from the cover” (Lydon, “How” 287). In his Yale _Daily News_ column, he lambasted the Beatles as “poor foreign imitations” who made him scream for Chuck Berry and Elvis (“Michael,” _Yale_). After graduation, he went to work for _Newsweek_, who immediately assigned him to London. He interviewed Lennon and McCartney upon the release of _Rubber Soul_, the 1965 album which converted Michael to Beatles fandom: “_Rubber Soul_ … marks a turning away from the percussive electric backgrounds of rhythm and blues to more intimate settings and subtler forms. … [T]heir lyrics are no longer concerned with handholding, but with desertion, seduction, and satire” (Lydon, “Bards” 102). In his interview, he found Paul “almost too charming” (“Bio”) preferring John’s “combative confidence” (“How” 292). Interestingly, Paul told him, “I wouldn’t mind being a white-haired old man writing songs … but I’d hate to be a white-haired Beatle playing at Empress Stadium” (“Bards” 102).

Michael was not an immediate fan of Bob Dylan either. He found Dylan’s early releases to be “too serious … raw, amateurish, and naïve” (_Busy_ 73). For Michael, Dylan did not achieve greatness until his sixth album, 1965’s _Highway 61 Revisited_, “his savage masterpiece” (“How” 289). That same summer he recognized the brilliance of the Stones with “Satisfaction.” Over the years, Michael referred to the Beatles, Dylan, and the Stones as the “troika” (see, e.g., _Busy_ 153) or “the Big Three” (e.g., _Flashbacks_ 127), “who would dominate … free and inspire pop music. … giving us daring, breathtakingly original music that grew in confidence and beauty with every new album. … They made us dance, they made us think” (_Busy_ 153).

In 1967, _Newsweek_ sent Michael back to the States for the Monterey International Pop Festival. However, the magazine only published ten paragraphs of his 43-paragraph report. But it would be another article, a freelance piece, in _Esquire_ that brought Michael to the attention of Jann Wenner, who was developing a new magazine. At a late August 1967 coffeehouse meeting, Michael accepted Wenner’s offer to be a founding editor at _Rolling Stone_. Continuing his work at _Newsweek_, Michael wrote _Rolling Stone_’s first cover story, an investigation into Monterey and its questionable fundraising efforts. The festival, he found, looked “like the traditional Charity Ball in hippie drag” (“High Cost” 1). In 1968, Michael decided to leave both _Newsweek_ and _Rolling Stone_ and strike out as a freelancer.

In 1969, _The New York Times_ commissioned Michael to cover the American tour of the Rolling Stones. It proved to be a life-altering experience. He grew tired of the competitiveness of journalists, who measured their success by whether they rode back to the hotel or the airport in a limousine with one of the Stones. He once told me that he complimented Keith Richards’s performance one night. Richards responded insecurely, “You think so?” At that moment, Michael realized that the Stones were “incredibly hard-working cats … passionate about music and filled with provocative ideas” (personal interview) but not, as he wrote, “the impervious rockstar[s] I and other fans and rock writers had helped create. [Keith] was another guy like me, and, in his own way, just as nervous as I was” (_Flashbacks_ 124). While the _Times_ did not publish Michael’s report, it was later included in _Rock Folk_ and _Flashbacks_.

Shortly after the tour, Michael started playing the guitar. Over time he would develop into a very good guitarist, giving lessons at various schools, while also writing songs and recording several albums. He first took the stage around 1970 with Ellen Mandel, an accomplished pianist, who would become his wife. In 1974, he and Ellen moved to New York City, where Ellen still resides and remains active in the Manhattan theater and club circuits. She has created music and sound design for approximately 100 plays and recorded several albums. Michael, who promoted himself as “The Handsomest Man in the World,” relished performing, but he never dropped his pen. Among his many books are _Rock Folk_ (1971), _Boogie Lightning_ (1974), _Writing and Life_ (1995), _Ray Charles: Man and Music_ (1998), _Flashbacks_ (2003), and _Busy Being Born_ (2018). Insiders working on the film _Ray_ (2004) privately disclosed to Michael, after Charles’s death, that the film would not have been possible without _Man and Music_. Charles was angry with some of the revelations in the book and forbade anyone involved with the film from speaking to Michael. In December 2025, a tribute concert to Michael was held at NYC’s Triad Theater, in which numerous performers from the New York City stage and cabaret scene performed his songs and read excerpts from his writings.

I first met Michael in 2004 when we were judges in a Battle of the Bands at the Bitter End, Greenwich Village, a contest sponsored by the New York Blues and Jazz Society with the winner advancing to the finals in the International Blues Challenge in Memphis. I had read Michael’s work for years and recently read his Ray Charles book. To me, Michael was a legend. That night, I talked to him every chance I could, and he indulged me. I don’t know if he knew this, but as we exited the club, instead of my walking west to get the F train at the W. 4 th Street station, I walked with him to the East Village and got the F at 2 nd Ave. I just wanted to talk with him.

In short time, we became friends. He introduced me to his editor at Routledge, who became my first editor there, and Michael tutored me on how to negotiate with publishers. Somehow, however, “Tom Kitts” did not carry the same clout as “Michael Lydon.” Another time I submitted an article to a journal on the films of Monterey Pop, Woodstock, and Altamont. I was asked to revise the article with one reviewer recommending that, “if possible,” I should interview someone at Altamont. Within a couple of days, I got together with Michael, who took out his scrapbook, and gave me sensational quotations about the dark vibe at the festival. “There was a grimness and a scariness that was palatable,” he said. “I went to the grounds the night before and I saw kids that seemed homeless, aimless, ruthless—unlike the hippies at Monterey, many of whom were really smart college kids. There was an ugliness at Altamont that was frightening” (qtd. in Kitts 727–28). In my acceptance letter, the reviewer wrote that I “hit a home run” by “somehow” connecting with Lydon.

But what I am most proud of in my relationship with Michael is that I recruited him to teach an undergraduate course for my department. We were having lunch when, as chair, I asked him to teach ENG 1074, Writing about Music. He was enthusiastic, but not about that class. He asked if he could develop his own class, which he did. He taught The Music of Writing for some dozen years. He was outstanding as I observed and as his reviews attest: “Prof Lydon is the best! English for three hours seems like a drag. Nope, not here,” wrote one student. “You sing at the beg. of every class!” Another student wrote, “Take him if you can; it’s a life changing experience!” (“Michael Lydon,” _Rate_). One afternoon, in February 2019, Michael and Wayne Robins, another prominent music journalist, editor, professor at SJU, and member of the _RMS_ editorial board, sat before an overflow crowd on our campus for a joint interview by Prof. Lawrence Pitilli, which was published in _Rock Music Studies_ (Pitilli). In addition to his article on the Beatles, cited above, Michael also wrote about Chuck Berry in 2019 for our journal (“Chuck”).

Once or twice a year, Michael and Ellen and my wife Lisa and I would get together for dinner at usually one of the remaining Ukrainian restaurants in the East Village. Among other things, Michael talked about his latest teaching innovation, his gifted and ambitious students, and his, let’s say, not-so-ambitious students. He loved being a professor. It was, however, when we were scheduling a dinner that Ellen informed me that his Parkinson’s had worsened and that he was no longer able to dine out. Michael passed away on 30 July 2025, at age 82, survived by Ellen, his daughter Shuna from his first marriage, and many friends.

# Michael Lydon (1943–2025)

[Thomas M. Kitts](https://www.tandfonline.com/author/Kitts%2C+Thomas+M)St. John’s University Correspondence[kittst@stjohns.edu](mailto:kittst@stjohns.edu)
