Michael Lydon had a storied career as a music journalist. He interviewed the Beatles, toured with the Rollings Stones and B.B. King, covered the Monterey International Pop Festival and Altamont, was a founding editor of _Rolling Stone_, considered Jerry Garcia and Janis Joplin his Haight-Ashbury inside sources, and wrote several books on music and writing. He was also a contributor to this journal and member of our editorial board. Michael passed away during the summer of 2025.

As a student at Yale in 1964, Michael said that he “begged everybody to listen to my jazz records, but all anyone wanted to hear was the stupid blue-black LP with the four jerks staring blankly out from the cover” (Lydon, “How” 287). In his Yale _Daily News_ column, he lambasted the Beatles as “poor foreign imitations” who made him scream for Chuck Berry and Elvis (“Michael,” _Yale_). After graduation, he went to work for _Newsweek_, who immediately assigned him to London. He interviewed Lennon and McCartney upon the release of _Rubber Soul_, the 1965 album which converted Michael to Beatles fandom: “_Rubber Soul_ … marks a turning away from the percussive electric backgrounds of rhythm and blues to more intimate settings and subtler forms. … [T]heir lyrics are no longer concerned with handholding, but with desertion, seduction, and satire” (Lydon, “Bards” 102). In his interview, he found Paul “almost too charming” (“Bio”) preferring John’s “combative confidence” (“How” 292). Interestingly, Paul told him, “I wouldn’t mind being a white-haired old man writing songs … but I’d hate to be a white-haired Beatle playing at Empress Stadium” (“Bards” 102).

Michael was not an immediate fan of Bob Dylan either. He found Dylan’s early releases to be “too serious … raw, amateurish, and naïve” (_Busy_ 73). For Michael, Dylan did not achieve greatness until his sixth album, 1965’s _Highway 61 Revisited_, “his savage masterpiece” (“How” 289). That same summer he recognized the brilliance of the Stones with “Satisfaction.” Over the years, Michael referred to the Beatles, Dylan, and the Stones as the “troika” (see, e.g., _Busy_ 153) or “the Big Three” (e.g., _Flashbacks_ 127), “who would dominate … free and inspire pop music. … giving us daring, breathtakingly original music that grew in confidence and beauty with every new album. … They made us dance, they made us think” (_Busy_ 153).

In 1967, _Newsweek_ sent Michael back to the States for the Monterey International Pop Festival. However, the magazine only published ten paragraphs of his 43-paragraph report. But it would be another article, a freelance piece, in _Esquire_ that brought Michael to the attention of Jann Wenner, who was developing a new magazine. At a late August 1967 coffeehouse meeting, Michael accepted Wenner’s offer to be a founding editor at _Rolling Stone_. Continuing his work at _Newsweek_, Michael wrote _Rolling Stone_’s first cover story, an investigation into Monterey and its questionable fundraising efforts. The festival, he found, looked “like the traditional Charity Ball in hippie drag” (“High Cost” 1). In 1968, Michael decided to leave both _Newsweek_ and _Rolling Stone_ and strike out as a freelancer.

In 1969, _The New York Times_ commissioned Michael to cover the American tour of the Rolling Stones. It proved to be a life-altering experience. He grew tired of the competitiveness of journalists, who measured their success by whether they rode back to the hotel or the airport in a limousine with one of the Stones. He once told me that he complimented Keith Richards’s performance one night. Richards responded insecurely, “You think so?” At that moment, Michael realized that the Stones were “incredibly hard-working cats … passionate about music and filled with provocative ideas” (personal interview) but not, as he wrote, “the impervious rockstar[s] I and other fans and rock writers had helped create. [Keith] was another guy like me, and, in his own way, just as nervous as I was” (_Flashbacks_ 124). While the _Times_ did not publish Michael’s report, it was later included in _Rock Folk_ and _Flashbacks_.

Shortly after the tour, Michael started playing the guitar. Over time he would develop into a very good guitarist, giving lessons at various schools, while also writing songs and recording several albums. He first took the stage around 1970 with Ellen Mandel, an accomplished pianist, who would become his wife. In 1974, he and Ellen moved to New York City, where Ellen still resides and remains active in the Manhattan theater and club circuits. She has created music and sound design for approximately 100 plays and recorded several albums. Michael, who promoted himself as “The Handsomest Man in the World,” relished performing, but he never dropped his pen. Among his many books are _Rock Folk_ (1971), _Boogie Lightning_ (1974), _Writing and Life_ (1995), _Ray Charles: Man and Music_ (1998), _Flashbacks_ (2003), and _Busy Being Born_ (2018). Insiders working on the film _Ray_ (2004) privately disclosed to Michael, after Charles’s death, that the film would not have been possible without _Man and Music_. Charles was angry with some of the revelations in the book and forbade anyone involved with the film from speaking to Michael. In December 2025, a tribute concert to Michael was held at NYC’s Triad Theater, in which numerous performers from the New York City stage and cabaret scene performed his songs and read excerpts from his writings.

I first met Michael in 2004 when we were judges in a Battle of the Bands at the Bitter End, Greenwich Village, a contest sponsored by the New York Blues and Jazz Society with the winner advancing to the finals in the International Blues Challenge in Memphis. I had read Michael’s work for years and recently read his Ray Charles book. To me, Michael was a legend. That night, I talked to him every chance I could, and he indulged me. I don’t know if he knew this, but as we exited the club, instead of my walking west to get the F train at the W. 4 th Street station, I walked with him to the East Village and got the F at 2 nd Ave. I just wanted to talk with him.

In short time, we became friends. He introduced me to his editor at Routledge, who became my first editor there, and Michael tutored me on how to negotiate with publishers. Somehow, however, “Tom Kitts” did not carry the same clout as “Michael Lydon.” Another time I submitted an article to a journal on the films of Monterey Pop, Woodstock, and Altamont. I was asked to revise the article with one reviewer recommending that, “if possible,” I should interview someone at Altamont. Within a couple of days, I got together with Michael, who took out his scrapbook, and gave me sensational quotations about the dark vibe at the festival. “There was a grimness and a scariness that was palatable,” he said. “I went to the grounds the night before and I saw kids that seemed homeless, aimless, ruthless—unlike the hippies at Monterey, many of whom were really smart college kids. There was an ugliness at Altamont that was frightening” (qtd. in Kitts 727–28). In my acceptance letter, the reviewer wrote that I “hit a home run” by “somehow” connecting with Lydon.

But what I am most proud of in my relationship with Michael is that I recruited him to teach an undergraduate course for my department. We were having lunch when, as chair, I asked him to teach ENG 1074, Writing about Music. He was enthusiastic, but not about that class. He asked if he could develop his own class, which he did. He taught The Music of Writing for some dozen years. He was outstanding as I observed and as his reviews attest: “Prof Lydon is the best! English for three hours seems like a drag. Nope, not here,” wrote one student. “You sing at the beg. of every class!” Another student wrote, “Take him if you can; it’s a life changing experience!” (“Michael Lydon,” _Rate_). One afternoon, in February 2019, Michael and Wayne Robins, another prominent music journalist, editor, professor at SJU, and member of the _RMS_ editorial board, sat before an overflow crowd on our campus for a joint interview by Prof. Lawrence Pitilli, which was published in _Rock Music Studies_ (Pitilli). In addition to his article on the Beatles, cited above, Michael also wrote about Chuck Berry in 2019 for our journal (“Chuck”).

Once or twice a year, Michael and Ellen and my wife Lisa and I would get together for dinner at usually one of the remaining Ukrainian restaurants in the East Village. Among other things, Michael talked about his latest teaching innovation, his gifted and ambitious students, and his, let’s say, not-so-ambitious students. He loved being a professor. It was, however, when we were scheduling a dinner that Ellen informed me that his Parkinson’s had worsened and that he was no longer able to dine out. Michael passed away on 30 July 2025, at age 82, survived by Ellen, his daughter Shuna from his first marriage, and many friends.

**Principal and Co-Founder of Street Plans | USA**

Mike Lydon runs Street Plans, a company that works with government and community partners to plan, design, and implement more sustainable and inclusive streets and public spaces.

By applying tactical urbanism methodology, Street Plans physically and iteratively transform streets and other public spaces together with clients and, crucially, the residents of the city. As cities are where the majority of humans reside, Mike believes that this is where the most social and economic opportunity for improvement can be found. “We must protect and enhance cities,” he says, “so that the human habitat is constantly evolving to meet human need.”

### Design for the Just City (02:30)

![Image 2: Toni Griffin](https://iqc.ou.edu/wp-content/uploads/2017/07/griffin.jpg)

#### Toni Griffin

Urban Planning for the American City

Toni L. Griffin works with cities as the founder of [Urban Planning for the American City](http://www.planningamericancity.com/about-us), with projects including Detroit Future City, a comprehensive citywide framework for urban transformation. She is developing values-based planning methodologies through the Just City Design Lab at the Harvard Graduate School of Design.

*   [X](http://twitter.com/tonilgriffin)

### Tactical Urbanism (30:00)

![Image 3: Mike Lydon](https://iqc.ou.edu/wp-content/uploads/2017/07/lydon.jpg)

#### Mike Lydon

Street Plans Collaborative

Mike Lydon is a Principal of [The Street Plans Collaborative](http://www.street-plans.com/), an international award-winning planning, design, and research-advocacy firm based in Miami, New York City, and San Francisco. With Tony Garcia, Mike is the recipient of the [2017 Seaside Prize](http://www.seasideinstitute.org/new-events/2016/10/17/seaside-prize) and co-author of [Tactical Urbanism: Short-term Action for Long-term Change](https://islandpress.org/book/tactical-urbanism), published by Island Press in 2015 and named by Planetizen as one of the top 10 planning books of the year.

### Design for the Just City (02:30)

![Image 2: Toni Griffin](https://iqc.ou.edu/wp-content/uploads/2017/07/griffin.jpg)

#### Toni Griffin

Urban Planning for the American City

Toni L. Griffin works with cities as the founder of [Urban Planning for the American City](http://www.planningamericancity.com/about-us), with projects including Detroit Future City, a comprehensive citywide framework for urban transformation. She is developing values-based planning methodologies through the Just City Design Lab at the Harvard Graduate School of Design.

*   [X](http://twitter.com/tonilgriffin)

### Tactical Urbanism (30:00)

![Image 3: Mike Lydon](https://iqc.ou.edu/wp-content/uploads/2017/07/lydon.jpg)

#### Mike Lydon

Street Plans Collaborative

Mike Lydon is a Principal of [The Street Plans Collaborative](http://www.street-plans.com/), an international award-winning planning, design, and research-advocacy firm based in Miami, New York City, and San Francisco. With Tony Garcia, Mike is the recipient of the [2017 Seaside Prize](http://www.seasideinstitute.org/new-events/2016/10/17/seaside-prize) and co-author of [Tactical Urbanism: Short-term Action for Long-term Change](https://islandpress.org/book/tactical-urbanism), published by Island Press in 2015 and named by Planetizen as one of the top 10 planning books of the year.
